note: Brock Purdy was awesome out of the gate for fantasy as the QB10 last week. Among 32 qualifying passers, Purdy was 23rd in yards per attempt, sixth-best in passing success rate, second in catchable target rate, and eighth in hero throw rate. Purdy also added five rushing attempts and 29 yards on the ground in Week 1. Purdy's rushing equity is also a nice cherry on top of the fantasy cake. In four of his nine games started last season, he had at least 20 rushing yards or a rushing score. Purdy should post strong QB1 numbers again this week. In Week 1, Miami allowed three passing scores to Kirk Cousins while generating pressure on only 6.5% of his dropbacks. Purdy should enjoy clean pockets all game and pick apart the Dolphins' secondary.

This wasn't the start to the season that many envisioned for Justin Herbert and the Bolts' offense. Herbert was the QB22 for the week. He threw for only 209 yards and one score (one interception). Herbert added 29 yards on the ground with five carries. Herbert was very accurate as a passer despite their offensive shortcomings. Among 32 qualifying passers for Week 1, Herbert was 13th in yards per attempt, third-best in highly accurate throw rate, and seventh in catchable target rate. I expect him to bounce back in Week 2. The question is how much for fantasy purposes. The Raiders faced Malik Willis and the Dolphins in Week 1, so it's tough to take much away from the pass defense. Last year, Las Vegas allowed the ninth-highest passing success rate, the tenth-highest passer rating, and the tenth-most EPA per dropback. I view this as a middle-of-the-road matchup at worst for Herbert in Week 2.

Trevor Lawrence began the 2026 season with a wonderful performance against the Browns as QB5 for the week. In Week 1, among 32 qualifying passers, Lawrence was third in yards per attempt, first in passing success rate, fourth in catchable target rate, and 14th in hero throw rate. I know it's obvious, but the Browns aren't the Broncos. This will be a tougher test for Lawrence in Week 2 than Cleveland could conjure up in Week 1. Lawrence shredded this pass defense last year to the tune of a QB2 finish for the week (31.2 points) with 279 passing yards, 7.8 yards per attempt, three passing scores, 20 rushing yards, and a rushing score. Denver wasn't a shutdown defense in Week 1, ranking 15th in passing success rate and 16th in EPA per dropback, so it's possible Lawrence, who looked in midseason form in Week 1, could have another strong day in Week 2.

Even Drake Maye's rushing ability (seven carries and 47 rushing yards) couldn't help him escape QB2 land in Week 1 (QB23 in weekly scoring). Maye struggled against an elite Seattle pass defense, and losing his alpha receiver AJ Brown during the game didn't help. Among 30 qualifying passers, Maye was 24th in yards per attempt and passing success rate, 14th in highly accurate throw rate, and 16th in EPA per dropback. We'll see if Maye can bounce back in Week 2 against a Pittsburgh pass defense that wasn't tested in Week 1. Yes, in Week 1 the Steelers allowed the 12th-fewest yards per attempt, the lowest passer rating, and the second-lowest passing success rate, but they also faced Cooper Rush. Take those pass defense stats with a grain of salt, although it is noteworthy that against Rush they had the 12th-lowest pressure rate. I expect Maye to have a better Week 2. The question is how much better.

Jaxson Dart picked up right where he left off last season as the QB4 in fantasy in Week 1. He finished Week 1 second in rushing yards among quarterbacks, behind only Caleb Williams. Among 30 qualifying passers, Dart was 12th in yards per attempt, second in passing success rate, eighth in highly accurate throw rate, and 14th in catchable target rate. Dart should see plenty of clean pockets in Week 2 against a Rams' pass rush that will be without Myles Garrett and had the ninth-lowest pressure rate with him in Week 1. Dart should have another strong outing in Week 2 against a pass defense that in Week 1 allowed the sixth-highest passing success rate, the tenth-highest passer rating, and the 11th-highest EPA per dropback.

Well, it happened. The unthinkable. Andy Reid directed a run-balanced offense in Week 1 with Patrick Mahomes under center as Mahomes attempted only 27 passes. Mahomes was surprisingly spry in the pocket and added seventh rushing attempts, 23 rushing yards, and a rushing score. This helped vault Mahomes to QB9 for the week in fantasy. Mahomes didn't play well, though, as he continued his dink-and-dunk ways and wasn't accurate while doing so. Among 32 qualifying quarterbacks in Week 1, he had the 13th-lowest yards per attempt, the second-lowest aDOT (4.45), the fifth-lowest catchable target rate, and the ninth-highest off-target rate. We'll see if Mahomes can turn it around in Week 2 against a pass defense that Lamar Jackson shredded in Week 1. In Week 1, Indy allowed the highest yards per attempt, the fourth-highest passer rating, and the fifth-highest passing success rate.

In Week 1, Jared Goff in a shootout finished as QB16 in fantasy. Among 30 qualifying quarterbacks, he was 27th in yards per attempt and had the seventh-lowest aDOT while finishing 13th in passing success rate, tenth in highly accurate throw rate, and eighth in catchable target rate. Yes, the low aDOT helped the accuracy metrics, no doubt. This Lions' offense remained reliant upon the "easy button" ideas that we love in Week 1, as they were third in motion rate (75%) and seventh in play action rate. The Bills' pass defense struggled in Week 1 and could again versus the Lions.. In Week 1, they ranked 18th in yards per attempt while allowing the ninth-highest passer rating, the 14th-highest EPA per dropback, and sporting the 13th-lowest pressure rate. Last year, Buffalo allowed the eighth-highest passing success rate and ranked 15th in passer rating when dealing with play-action. I expect Goff to have a bounce-back game in Week 2.

Matthew Stafford was abysmal in Week 1. I'm sorry, but there's no other way to state it. Stafford was erratic, to put it kindly, as he was misfiring left and right. He finished the week as QB32 in fantasy. Among 30 qualifying passers, he had the tenth-fewest yards per attempt, the fifth-lowest passing success rate, the fifth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the sixth-lowest catchable target rate. In his defense, he did face the eighth-highest pressure rate in Week 1, but that's no excuse. Stafford needs a big bounceback game in Week 2, and I don't know if it's coming. The Giants more than held their own as a defense last week against the Cowboys. They allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt and the ninth-lowest passer rating while ranking 17th in passing success rate and 18th in pressure rate. I need to see Stafford bounce back before I'm willing to plug him back into a fantasy lineup. He has zero rushing equity to save his fantasy day if he is horrible as a passer again.

Jordan Love had a busy day slinging it in Week 1 with uneven results. He attempted the second-most passes in Week 1 (42) with the second-most passing yards (387), but his per-dropback metrics were horrible. Among 32 qualifying passers, he was seventh in yards per attempt and had the ninth-highest aDOT (10.4), but he was 12th-lowest in passing success rate, second-worst in highly accurate throw rate, and had the highest off-target rate. Not good, Bob. I'm worried about Love in Week 2. Last week, the Jets allowed the fewest yards per attempt, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, and the tenth-lowest EPA per dropback. I will also say that these numbers were accumulated against Cam Ward, who has a strong case as a bottom-five quarterback in the NFL right now. Take them with a grain of salt for Week 2. My worries about Love really reside more with Love than with believing in the Jets' pass defense after one game.

Baker Mayfield had butter hands in Week 1, and it cost the Bucs. Mayfield had THREE fumbles in Week 1. He flopped for fantasy as the QB27 for the week. He added 30 rushing yards and a score on the ground, but it wasn't enough to save his fantasy day. As a passer, he was strong (among 32 qualifying passers), ranking 14th in yards per attempt, third in passing success rate and catchable target rate, and 17th in highly accurate throw rate. Mayfield should go full savage mode in Week 2 against his former team that ran him out of town after he played hurt during his tenure. Last week, Cleveland allowed the third-most yards per attempt, the highest passer rating, and the highest passing success rate.

Bo Nix looked lost in Week 1 as the QB31 in fantasy. Among 32 qualifying passers, he had the second-fewest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the third-lowest EPA per dropback, and he ranked 18th in highly accurate throw rate. He'll have another difficult task in Week 2, facing a Jacksonville pass defense that last season allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest passing success rate, and the fifth-lowest passer rating. I don't have high hopes for NIx this week, as the Denver offense and their new play caller, Davis Webb, seem to have a ton to iron out before this offense is humming again.

Tyler Shough looked lost in the first half of Week 1's game against the Lions, but thankfully he remembered how to play football in the second half and settled down. He finished the week as the QB6 in fantasy with 410 passing yards and three passing scores (two picks). Shough led the entire NFL with 56 passing attempts. I don't expect that to be a weekly occurrence. Among 32 qualifying passers, he was 16th in yards per attempt, 17th in passing success rate, 26th in highly accurate throw rate, and third in hero throw rate. Shough could see a hefty amount of passing volume again this week if the Saints fall behind early against the Ravens, but this defense won't be quite as easy as Detroit's to pass against. In Week 1, Baltimore allowed the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passer rating, and the seventh-lowest passing success rate while generating the 11th-best pressure rate.

Bryce Young went off in Week 1 against the hapless Bears pass defense as the QB3 for the week. Young directed an offense that had the fifth-highest passing rate. We'll see if that trend holds as we move through the season, but after one game it's notable. Among 32 qualified passers in Week 1, Young was fourth in yards per attempt, seventh in passing success rate, and ninth in hero throw rate, but it wasn't all glitz and glam for Young as he was also 23rd in highly accurate throw rate and 27th in catchable target rate. It was a nice showing for Young, but I'm not ready to say this is some new version of Young who could set the league on fire in 2026. We'll see how Young holds up this week against an Atlanta pass defense that played well against Aaron Rodgers in Week 1. Last week, Atlanta allowed the ninth-fewest yards per attempt, the fifth-lowest passing success rate, and the eighth-lowest passer rating.

C.J. Stroud had a strong Week 1 against a talented Bills' pass defense as the QB14 for the week. Among 30 qualifying receivers, he was 18th in yards per attempt, tenth in passing success rate and hero throw rate, had the highest accurate throw rate, and he had the 12th-lowest aDOT (7.7). It was an encouraging outing for Stroud and arguably the best he's played over the last few seasons after his standout rookie season. Stroud could stack another solid outing in Week 2 against this new-look Cincy pass defense. In Week 1, Cincy allowed the 14th-highest yards per attempt and the third-highest passing success rate and CPOE. Cincy ranked 15th in pressure rate in Week 1, which isn't otherworldly. Houston's offensive line held up well in Week 1 as Stroud faced the 13th-lowest pressure rate, so Stroud should see plenty of clean pockets in Week 2.

Malik Willis began the season with a strong fantasy finish as the QB12 for the week. It was based on his rushing, as Willis had 39 rushing yards and a score. That was the sixth-most rushing yards in Week 1 for a quarterback. Willis began the game looking solid as a passer before things unraveled. Willis dealt with the tenth-highest pressure rate among Week 1 quarterbacks, which played into it, but Willis wasn't accurate outside of that. Among 30 qualifying passers in Week 1, Willis was tenth in yards per attempt and sixth in hero throw rate, displaying the arm talent that he has, but he was also 21st in passing success rate, 20th in highly accurate throw rate, and he had the sixth-highest off-target rate. Willis will have a tough time in Week 2 against a revitalized 49ers' pass defense that made the Rams look like a junior high school offense in Week 1. In Week 1, the 49ers allowed the third-lowest EPA per dropback, the ninth-fewest yards per attempt, the eighth-lowest passing success rate, and they generated the fourth-highest pressure rate. Willis will need a big day in the rushing department again to carry his fantasy day.

Carson Wentz will draw the start for Minnesota this week as Kyler Murray isn't ready to go yet after sustaining a concussion in Week 1. Last week, Wentz finished as the QB12 for fantasy, but it wasn't all sunshine and roses for Wentz. On a per-dropback basis, he struggled with accuracy. Among 32 qualifying quarterbacks, he was 19th in yards per attempt and passing success rate. Wentz also had the seventh-highest off-target rate and the eighth-lowest catchable target rate. Despite his accuracy issues, Wentz could post another nice stat line this week against Chicago's struggling pass defense. Last week, Chicago allowed the fourth-most yards per attempt, the ninth-highest passing success rate and passer rating, and the eighth-most EPA per dropback.

Daniel Jones was a statue in Week 1, running only once for four yards as he limped to a QB28 fantasy finish for Week 1. He also struggled mightily in his first game back as a passer. Among 32 qualifying passers in Week 1, Jones had the seventh-lowest yards per attempt and passing success rate, the 12th-lowest aDOT, the 14th-lowest catchable target rate, and the 13th-highest off-target rate. Jones will have a tough road to walk in Week 2 against a pass defense that had Bo Nix in a blender. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the second-fewest yards per attempt, the fifth-lowest passer rating, and the fourth-lowest passing success rate. The Chiefs also led the NFL in Week 1 with a wild 54.5% pressure rate. I expect Jones to be under duress in Week 2.

Jacoby Brissett had a solid outing in Week 1 as the QB15 in fantasy. Among 32 qualifying passers, he was 15th in yards per attempt, eighth in passing success rate, fifth in catchable target rate, and sixth in highly accurate throw rate. He'll have a longer day against this talented Seattle pass defense. Brissett attempted the seventh-most pass attempts in Week 1, and I expect him to remain pass heavy so the volume will be there for Brissett to churn out some production. In Week 1, Seattle allowed the eighth-fewest yards per attempt, the eighth-lowest passing success rate, and the second-lowest passer rating.

Last week, Geno Smith was the QB29 in fantasy. That finish has more to do with the fact that Smith doesn't run and he didn't throw any passing touchdowns than with his play being poor. Last week, among 32 qualifying passers, Smith was eighth in yards per attempt, 14th in passing success rate, second in highly accurate throw rate, and fifth in hero throw rate. We'll see how Smith fares in Week 2, but he should be able to cobble together a stat line that should return solid QB2 value. Last week, Green Bay allowed the 12th-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passing success rate, and they ranked 16th in EPA per dropback. This was also against Carson Wentz, so take all of it with a grain of salt. I look at this as a neutral matchup for Smith.

After one game of the 2026 season, it looks like low aDOT Aaron Rodgers is gone. Last year, after operating as a checkdown king, Rodgers had the tenth-highest aDOT in Week 1, but the results weren't any better as he was the QB25 in fantasy. Among 30 qualifying passers, Rodgers had the eighth-lowest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the 13th-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and he ranked 15th in catchable target rate. Rodgers could post a better stat line in Week 2, but that's a low bar to clear. In Week 1, against Drew Lock, the Pats allowed the ninth-most yards per attempt and passing success rate and the seventh-highest passer rating. Rodgers could take advantage in Week 2, but this defense also had the fifth-best pressure rate. At this stage of his career, Rodgers isn't the most mobile quarterback. If the Pats pass rush can get home early and often, it could be a long day for Rodgers.

Last week, Kirk Cousins was the QB18 in fantasy as he played game manager against one of the league's worst defenses. Among 32 qualifying passers last week, Cousins had the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest passing success rate, the 13th-lowest aDOT, and the 11th-highest off-target rate. Cousins should put up another decent QB2 stat line for Week 2. Last week, the Chargers allowed the seventh-highest passing success rate, the ninth-most EPA per dropback, and they ranked 15th in yards per attempt.

Drew Lock will draw a few more starts for Seattle as Sam Darnold recovers from his Week 1 injury. In Week 1, Lock was the QB23 in fantasy. Among 32 qualifying passers, he ranked ninth in yards per attempt, ninth in passing success rate, 21st in catchable target rate, and he had the fifth-highest off-target rate. He'll tangle with a Cards pass defense that allowed the 13th-most yards per attempt in Week 1, but they also held the Bolts to the 12th-lowest passing success rate and ninth-fewest EPA per dropback. Lock should be considered a low-end QB2.

Cam Ward in Week 1 looked very similar to 2025 Cam Ward as the QB25 in fantasy. He had only 140 passing yards with a pitiful 4.3 yards per attempt, zero hero throws, a 50% highly accurate throw rate, and a 68.8% catchable target rate. None of this is good. Also add in that he was pressured on 46.2% of his dropbacks, and the concern level reaches critical mass. The Eagles' pass defense will crush Ward in Week 2. In Week 1, they allowed the second-fewest yards per attempt, the third-lowest passing success rate, and ranked 11th in pressure rate.

The answer if you're considering playing Deshaun Watson in any format is just...no. Last week, he was the QB21 in fantasy while finishing with the fourth-highest off-target rate and the second-highest turnover-worthy play rate. I won't waste my time delving into this further or yours having to read a long blurb about Watson. I wouldn't be surprised if Watson is benched at some point this week. There's no way I'd start him in any format.

Atlanta will be running out Cooper Rush as their starter again this week. In Week 1, Rush was the QB30 in fantasy. I'll keep this short because no one should be starting Rush in any format. In Week 1, among 32 qualifying passers, Rush had the 12th-lowest yards per attempt, the second-lowest passing success rate, the fourth-lowest aDOT, and the lowest EPA per dropback. Don't roster Rush. Do not start him.

Last week, Breece Hall was the RB13 in fantasy, finishing with 24 touches and 118 total yards (one score). He played 60.3% of the snaps with 56.4% of the rushing attempts and a 30.8% route share (8.3% target share). He handled all four of the team's red zone rushing attempts. He had a solid 15% explosive run rate and a 14% missed tackle rate. Hall should see plenty of volume this week to help outkick a tougher matchup, but his overall stat line won't look as pretty as it did in Week 1. Last week, Green Bay allowed the lowest explosive run rate, the tenth-lowest rushing success rate, and the second-lowest missed tackle rate.

Kyren Williams remains the lead back for the Rams. Last week, he was the RB15, finishing with 14 touches (three receptions), 65 total yards, and a touchdown. He played 63.2% of the snaps and handled all four red zone rushing attempts with the starting offense. Williams wasn't an efficient runner in Week 1 with only 1.45 yards after contact per attempt and one missed tackle forced. Williams should be able to grind out another solid stat line in Week 2. In Week 1, the Giants allowed the third-highest rushing success rate and 13th-most yards after contact per attempt while sitting at 16th in stuff rate.

Last week, Bucky Irving finished as the RB15 in fantasy. He played 61.5% of the snaps for the Bucs while handling 53.3% of the designed rushing attempts. Irving finished with 15 touches and 93 total yards. Among 43 qualifying rushers, Irving was 20th in explosive run rate, tenth in yards after contact per attempt, and fifth-best in missed tackle rate. Irving was also the clear lead as the passing down back, handling a 58.3% route share with a 25% target share, 2.29 yards per route run, and 48 receiving yards. He should crush again this week. In Week 1, Cleveland allowed the fifth-highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the ninth-highest missed tackle rate.

David Montgomery was a volume monster in Week 1 as the RB5 in fantasy. He finished with 23 touches, 79 total yards, and three scores. He played 57.5% of the snaps, handled all five of the team's red zone carries, had a 42.9% route share, and a 7.9% target share (three targets). Montgomery wasn't immensely efficient with his work, but some of this is on his offensive line. Among 33 qualifying backs in Week 1, Montgomery was 18th in success rate and missed tackle rate, but he had the tenth-fewest yards before contact per attempt. Montgomery could find more running room in Week 2 against a Cincy run defense that allowed the fifth-highest rushing success rate and yards after contact per attempt in Week 1 while also having the 11th-lowest stuff rate.

Cam Skattebo started the season off with a solid showing as the RB18 in fantasy. He played 60.3% of the snaps, finishing with 18 rushing attempts and 81 rushing yards (one score). The human battering ram didn't garner a target, and he had a disappointing 30.3% route share. We'll have to see if this continues as we move through the season or if the Giants are simply easing him in. Among 33 qualifying rushers in Week 1, Skattebo ranked 15th in explosive run rate, 18th in yards after contact per attempt, and ninth-best in missed tackle rate. Skattebo should have another nice game in Week 2 against a run defense that allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the highest rushing success rate, and the highest yards before contact per attempt in Week 1. The Giants were third-best in yards before contact per attempt in Week 1. This new-look offensive line should be able to open holes for Skattebo in Week 2.

Rhamondre Stevenson was a volume RB2 in Week 1 as the RB17 in fantasy. With TreVeyon Henderson active in Week 2, I expect Stevenson to retain a similar workload and fantasy value. Last week, against an elite Seattle run defense, Stevenson played 85.1% of the snaps, finishing with 23 touches and 95 total yards. He drew an 18.1% target share and finished with 44 receiving yards. He had 2.50 yards after contact per attempt, essentially having to generate everything on the ground by himself as his offensive line only produced 0.33 yards before contact per attempt for him. Stevenson could see similar uphill sledding in Week 2 against a run defense that allowed the ninth-lowest explosive run rate, the sixth-lowest rushing success rate, and the 14th-lowest missed tackle rate in Week 1. Stevenson should have plenty of volume to outkick the tough matchup, though.

Chuba Hubbard remained Carolina's lead back to open the 2026 season as the RB10 for the week. Hubbard handled all three of Carolina's red zone rushing attempts while playing 67.7% of the snaps with a 52.6% designed carry share and 58.1% route share. Hubbard finished with 13 touches and 87 total yards. Among 43 qualifying rushers in Week 1, Hubbard was 19th in explosive run rate and 17th in missed tackle rate. Hubbard will have uphill sledding in Week 2 if the Falcons' run defense is as good as they showed in Week 1. Last week, they allowed the third-lowest explosive run rate, had the second-best stuff rate, and the eighth-lowest missed tackle rate. We'll see if Hubbard keeps this stranglehold on the workload for the Carolina backfield all season, but he is probably again the clear lead for the Panthers this week.

In Week 1, Jeremiyah Love split the workload with Tyler Allgeier, as he played 44.4% of the snaps with a 32.4% designed carry share, a 38.5% route share, and an 8.1% target share. Love had three red zone rushing attempts (Allgeier, three). Love got into the endzone which saved his day as the RB19 for the week. Love had 13 touches and 50 total yards. He was amazing on a per-touch basis with 4.0 yards after contact per attempt and a 27% missed tackle rate. Love will have a hard time finding running room in Week 2, so temper your expectations. In Week 1, Seattle allowed the 12th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-lowest rushing success rate, and they had the fifth-highest stuff rate.

In Week 1, Travis Etienne Jr. finished as the RB16 in PPR, rolling up 16 touches and 78 total yards. He played 59.3% of the snaps with a 36.5% route share, a 14.3% target share, 1.39 yards per route run, and 32 receiving yards. He matched Kendre Miller with a 39.1% designed carry share while producing a 22.2% explosive run rate and 22% missed tackle rate (NOICE!). He could have more volume on the ground in Week 2 if the Saints can keep this game close. Baltimore's run defense looked suspect in Week 1, allowing the highest explosive run rate, the 11th-best rushing success rate, and the tenth-most yards after contact per attempt.

In Week 1, Aaron Jones finished as the RB26 in fantasy. He had 12 touches and 40 total yards (one score) while playing 42.6% of the snaps with half of the running back red zone rushing attempts (four) and a 23.3% route share. Sadly, his per-touch metrics didn't look any better than last season's, as he had only 1.92 yards after contact per attempt and zero missed tackles forced. Jones could have another strong flex-worthy performance despite his inefficiencies in Week 2. With Jordan Mason out (thumb), Jones should be the clear lead back for the Vikings this week. The Bears' run defense was as poor in Week 1 as advertised this summer, allowing the eighth-highest explosive run rate, the second-highest rushing success rate, and the tenth-most EPA per rush.

Please, Seattle. Please. Utilize Jadarian Price more going forward. In Week 1, he played 50% of the snaps with 45.5% of the designed carries while seeing a 40.7% route share. He finished with 12 touches and 58 total scoreless yards. Price's juice and talent were easy to see. He had a 20% explosive run rate, a 20% missed tackle rate, and 2.90 yards after contact per attempt. Seattle should lean on him at least until Sam Darnold is back, but we'll see if that happens. In Week 1, Arizona allowed the third-most yards after contact per attempt and the third-highest missed tackle rate. Price should eat this week if Seattle is willing to feed him volume.

Quinshon Judkins was crushed by the Browns' anemic offense in Week 1 as the RB38 in fantasy. Judkins played 64.7% of the snaps, finishing with 14 touches and 40 total yards. Among 43 qualifying rushers, he ranked dead last in yards after contact per attempt, had zero explosive runs, and forced zero missed tackles. It was a rough outing for Judkins, and I don't know when it gets better with Deshaun Watson under center, but the Bucs' run defense struggled out of the gate last week, and if their Week 1 struggles are real, then maybe this is a low-key bounceback spot for Judkins. Last week, the Bucs allowed the 11th-highest rushing success rate, the ninth-most yards after contact per attempt, and they had the seventh-lowest stuff rate.

Jaylen Warren was the backup to Rico Dowdle in Week 1. Yes, if you look at the boxscore it doesn't look like that, as Warren finished with 15 touches and 73 total yards (Dowdle had ten touches) as the RB25 for the week, but he only played 35.9% of the snaps, had a 30.2% route share, and he didn't see any red zone rushing attempts. Yes, his fumble in the first quarter could have absolutely played a role in his reduced role for Week 1, but we'll have to see if that's the case if Dowdle massively out-snaps him in Week 2. When he was on the field, Warren was his same explosive self, posting 3.0 yards after contact per attempt. Warren could be an RB2 in Week 2 if he sees a similar workload against the Pats. In Week 1, New England allowed the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the 11th-most yards after contact per attempt, and they had the sixth-lowest stuff rate.

In Week 1, in a blowout game for Jacksonville, Bhayshul Tuten was the RB28 in fantasy, finishing with 16 touches and 88 total yards. He played 48.2% of the snaps with a 46.9% designed carry share and 33.3% route share (4.3% target share). Tuten looked good on early downs with a 20% explosive run rate and 33% missed tackle rate. Chris Rodriguez handled the only red zone rushing attempt for the backfield, so the concerns of Tuten getting "Kenneth Walker'd" at the goal line remain until we have a larger sample size of games. Tuten could have a massive game in Week 2 against a run defense that Kenneth Walker just ripped apart in Week 1. Last week, Denver allowed the tenth-highest explosive run rate, the highest yards after contact per attempt, and the highest missed tackle rate.

Last week, MarShawn Lloyd finished with a disappointing stat line with 13 carries and 37 rushing yards (zero receiving yards, one target). He played only 44.8% of the snaps while handling 61.9% of the team's designed carries. He had only a 15.2% route share and 2.4% target share. I hope his playing time increases this week, but it's not a sure thing as Chris Brooks could remain involved. Lloyd had only 1.38 yards after contact per attempt and zero missed tackles forced, but it's a one-game sample. I'm not freaking out about him after one game. Lloyd should find more running room this week against a run defense that in Week 1 allowed the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the fourth-highest rushing success rate, and the seventh-highest EPA per rush.

In Week 1, Bill was the RB22 in fantasy, seeing a 49.3% snap share and 55.2% of the designed carries. He finished with 17 touches and 65 total yards (one touchdown). Among 34 qualifying rushers, he was 14th in explosive run rate, 21st in yards after contact per attempt, and 22nd in rushing success rate. He had only one of Washington's five running back red zone carries, which is a problem, but it was one game, so we'll have to see if that continues. Bill was close behind Rachaad White in route share (34.2% vs. 36.8%). He only saw one target in the game. Bill is a solid flex that could return RB2 production again in Week 2. In Week 1, Dallas was 16th in rushing success rate allowed while giving up the eighth-most yards before contact per attempt and the 11th-highest missed tackle rate.

J.K. Dobbins reprised his early down only role in Week 1 to open the 2026 season. Dobbins played 40.4% of the snaps while handling 53.3% of the designed carries and seeing only a 15.2% route share. Dobbins finished with eight carries and 36 rushing yards. Dobbins will be a game-script-sensitive flex again this season. He did look like his normal self running the ball with a solid 12.5% explosive run rate and 3.5 yards after contact per attempt. Dobbins is a sit this week, though. I don't think gamescript is in his favor, and Jacksonville's run defense should be able to keep him from ripping off any big runs. Last week, Jacksonville allowed the second-lowest explosive run rate, the ninth-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and the sixth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Kenneth Gainwell is only a bench stash at this point. In Week 1, he played 45.6% of the snaps with only six touches and 18 total yards. Gainwell had only a 33.3% route share and a 3.6% target share in Week 1. Until his playing time increases, he's only a handcuff.

The Bears exploded for 59 points in Week 1, and with that offensive firepower output Kyle Monangai finished as the RB11 for the week. Monangai played 44.3% of the snaps with a 39.5% route share. He finished with 12 touches, 124 total yards, and a score. Monangai looked good in Week 1 with his touches popping off with a 22.2% explosive run rate and 7.5 yards after contact per attempt. We'll see if he can keep it up in Week 2 against what looks like a strong Minnesota run defense. In Week 1, Minnesota allowed the 14th-lowest explosive run rate, the fourth-lowest rushing success rate, and the 11th-fewest yards after contact per attempt. I expect Monangai to continue to be a touchdown-dependent RB3/flex option.

I know Rico Dowdle had only ten touches and 21 total yards in Week 1, but he was the starter for Pittsburgh. He led the backfield with a 57.8% snap rate, a 48.8% route share, and the only red zone carry. Yes, Jaylen Warren fumbled in the first quarter of their game against the Falcons, which could have played a part here, but we'll have to see the division of labor in Week 2. Dowdle wasn't amazing on a per-touch basis in Week 1 with only 1.75 yards after contact per attempt and a 13% missed tackle rate, but it's a small sample, and we have a much larger one over the last two seasons that shows Dowdle is #good. Dowdle has solid flex value this week in a good matchup. In Week 1, New England allowed the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the 11th-most yards after contact per attempt, and they had the sixth-lowest stuff rate.

RJ Harvey operated as the passing-down complement to J.K. Dobbins in Week 1. He played 55.3% of the snaps with a 42.4% route share. Harvey had a 14.3% target share and finished with seven touches and 41 total yards. Harvey is a viable PPR flex for Week 2. Last season, Jacksonville ranked 15th in yards per route run allowed to running backs while giving up the 11th-most receiving fantasy points per game to the position. Harvey popped up with a hamstring injury this week. Harvey didn't practice on Wednesday, but he did manage limited practice sessions on Thursday and Friday. He has been listed as questionable.

Tony Pollard had a disastrous Week 1 as he split the work with Tyjae Spears. Pollard was the RB41 in fantasy, finishing with eight touches and 34 total yards. He played 51% of the snaps with only a 17.9% route share (two targets, 6.3% target share). Pollard had zero red zone rushing attempts. He did post a respectable 2.43 yards after contact per attempt and saw 2.57 yards before contact per attempt, but he's essentially the early-down grinder for a woeful offense that isn't likely to sniff the red zone much in 2026. He faces a Philly run defense that allowed the 13th-lowest rushing success rate, the 11th-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and the 14th-fewest yards after contact per attempt in Week 1. Sit Pollard.

Blake Corum is a volatile flex play. He played only 22.8% of the snaps in Week 1 while seeing zero targets. His value is totally dependent upon what he does on early downs. Corum also didn't see a red zone rushing attempt in Week 1, so he'll likely have to break off a big run, which is possible. Corum looked like he was shot out of a cannon in Week 1 with a 20% explosive run rate and 20% missed tackle rate. I'm likely not rolling Corum out as a flex unless it's a deep league and I'm desperate. In Week 1, the Giants allowed the third-highest rushing success rate and the 13th-most yards after contact per attempt while sitting at 16th in stuff rate. If the Giants take the lead in this game, Corum could easily get gamescripted out.

In Week 1, Arizona had Tyler Allgeier leading the way as he saw a 56.9% snap rate, 50% of the designed carries, and a 38.5% route share (5.4% target share). Allgeier finished with 19 touches and 70 total yards as he split the red zone work with Jeremiyah Love. Each back had three red zone rushing attempts. Allgeier churned out a nice 2.59 yards after contact per attempt in Week 1 while recording a 12% missed tackle rate (meh). Allgeier will have to get by with volume this week because Seattle won't allow much breathing room on the ground. In Week 1, Seattle allowed the 12th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-lowest rushing success rate, and they had the fifth-highest stuff rate.

Kaelon Black operated as the 49ers' Blake Corum in Week 1 as an early-down complement to Christian McCaffrey. Black played 43.8% of the snaps finishing with 15 touches and 70 total yards (65 rushing yards). He wasn't impressive as a rusher, though. Among 33 qualifying rushers in Week 1, he was seventh in rushing success rate, but I attribute that to the 3.5 yards before contact per attempt that the offensive line generated for him. Among that same sample of backs, he was 32nd in yards after contact per attempt, and he didn't force a missed tackle. None of it probably matters in Week 2, though. Black will likely see a similar workload in Week 2 as I expect the 49ers to blow out the Dolphins, which means Black will get plenty of garbage time usage. Miami's run defense was predictably terrible in Week 1 as well. In Week 1, Miami allowed the seventh-highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the sixth-most yards after contact per attempt to backs. Black is a strong flex play for Week 2. Black popped up on the injury report this week with a groin issue. He did manage limited practice sessions on Thursday and Friday this week. He has been listed as questionable.

In Week 1, Rachaad White played 40.3% of the snaps for Washington with a 24.1% designed carry share. White finished the game with nine touches and 27 total yards. He had only one red zone rushing attempt (Washington had five total among the running backs). White edged out Bill in route share with 36.8% of the backfield routes (Bill, 34.2%). White wasn't efficient on the ground with zero explosive runs, 1.71 yards after contact per attempt, and zero missed tackles forced. White is a middling flex with a good matchup. In Week 1, Dallas was 16th in rushing success rate allowed while giving up the eighth-most yards before contact per attempt and the 11th-highest missed tackle rate.

Jonathon Brooks didn't see a heavy workload out of the gate for Carolina. We'll see how that evolves over time this season, but until his role grows, he's just a bench stash. Last week, he played 21% of the snaps with a 21.1% route share. Chuba Hubbard handled all of the red zone rushing work in Week 1. Brooks finished with five touches and 62 total yards. Don't flex Brooks until we see his workload increase. That could happen as early as this week, but we have to see it first.

TreVeyon Henderson opened the season with an ankle injury. It forced him to miss Week 1, but he opened this week with a full practice, so it looks like he'll be back for Week 2. Last year, TreVeyon Henderson finished his rookie season as the RB24 in fantasy points per game, but it wasn't nearly that productive for fantasy managers when you look at the full breakdown of how it unfolded. In Weeks 10-11, Rhamondre Stevenson wasn't active, and Henderson feasted with 60.3 combined PPR points, which accounted for 29.2% of his overall fantasy production for the season. If you take those two monster games out of the equation, Henderson would have averaged 9.8 PPR points per game, which would have made him the RB33 in fantasy points per game. Without Stevenson in the lineup in Weeks 9-11, Henderson averaged 19 touches and 110 total yards. With Stevenson active, Henderson had 11.2 touches and 57.2 total yards per game. This isn't to shade Henderson, but I'm trying to give context to his rookie season that will be overlooked at first glance. Last year, Henderson was bested by Stevenson in every metric that I care about, namely explosive run rate, missed tackle rate, yards after contact per attempt, yards per route run, and pass protection stats. Among 49 qualifying backs, Henderson ranked 12th in explosive run rate, but he was also 32nd in missed tackle rate and 42nd in yards after contact per attempt. Henderson is a middling flex with a bad matchup this week. Last week, Pittsburgh allowed the ninth-lowest explosive run rate, the sixth-lowest rushing success rate, and the 14th-lowest missed tackle rate.

In Week 1, Chris Rodriguez finished with six rushing attempts and 23 rushing yards as he played 41.1% of the snaps with an 18.8% designed carry share, a 29.2% route share, and zero targets. Rodriguez had the only red zone rushing attempt for the Jags in Week 1. Rodriguez had a respectable 2.33 yards after contact per attempt and a 17% missed tackle rate in Week 1. He's a touchdown-dependent flex play this week with what looks like a decent matchup. Last week, Denver allowed the tenth-highest explosive run rate, the highest yards after contact per attempt, and the highest missed tackle rate.

DeVonta Smith didn't have a massive Week 1 as the WR45 in weekly scoring. Hurts only threw the ball 25 times against the Commanders, so Smith's 20% target share (tied for the team lead) with a 23.5% first-read share didn't seem great. Smith finished with only three receptions and 53 receiving yards (1.83 YPRR, third on the team). Smith did see a deep target, but he didn't garner any red zone or end zone targets. Smith might not see a huge influx of volume in Week 2, but against the Titans he could easily be a WR2. In Week 1, Tennessee allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per target and the second-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Cordale Flott and Alontae Taylor weren't a formidable outside duo for Tennessee in Week 1, allowing a 118.8 passer rating and a 75% catch rate combined.

DJ Moore crushed all expectations in Week 1 as the Bills' new alpha wide receiver. He was the WR9 in weekly scoring, leading the team with a 24.1% target share and 33.3% first-read share while posting 100 receiving yards and three deep targets (zero red zone/end zone targets). I expect Moore to eat again in Week 2 against a Detroit secondary that allowed the 11th-most fantasy points per target and the seventh-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1.

In Week 1, after much speculation, Malik Nabers played and played well. He had only a 69.7% route share and 54.4% snap rate, but he turned that into a 31% target share and 36.4% first-read share. Nabers churned out 69 receiving yards and 3.0 yards per route run while drawing a red zone target. Nabers should see his playing time increase slightly in Week 2. With that bump in routes and his strong per-route efficiency, I wouldn't be shocked to see him produce as a WR2 this week. Last week, the Rams allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Rashee Rice had a touchdown in Week 1 to save his disappointing fantasy day as the WR36 for the week. Rice was almost a forgotten piece of the passing attack with a 7.4% target share (3.5 aDOT), 19 receiving yards (0.70 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 10% first-read share. His first-read share was third on the team behind Xavier Worthy and Travis Kelce. We'll see if Rice can bounce back this week against an Indy secondary that allowed the most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers in Week 1, but I'm not hopeful. Rice is a low aDOT drag route artist in what looks like a low or middling passing volume offense. This could be a high-volume passing offense again as Patrick Mahomes gets healthier and so does his offensive line as we move through the season, but I don't think we see that change in Week 1.

The 49ers' usage of their players was weird in some aspects in Week 1 because of the one-sided nature of the game, as they crushed the Rams. Mike Evans finished as the WR14 in weekly scoring, but he had only a 63.9% route share. This could also be related to the fact that Evans dealt with some nagging soft tissue stuff during camp, and San Francisco didn't want to run him out there for a 90% route share in Week 1. Evans still tied for the team lead with a 20.6% target share while producing 49 receiving yards (2.16 YPRR) and seeing a team-leading 24% first-read share. Evans was second on the team with two red zone targets. I don't expect the Miami Dolphins' youthful secondary to be able to contain Evans in Week 2. The Raiders didn't have to test them much in Week 1 and don't have the players to do so even if they wanted to. If Evans had his way with the Rams, I don't expect the Dolphins to be much of a problem.

In Week 1, Parker Washington operated as Jacksonville's WR1, finishing as the WR11 for the week. Washington had a 26.1% target share, 83 receiving yards (5.53 YPRR), zero red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 27.8% first-read share. The target share and first-read share easily led the team. The last time these two teams met, Washington had a 25% target share, 145 receiving yards, two red zone targets, a 23.8% first-read share, 26.5 PPR points, and a WR3 finish for the week. I expect Trevor Lawrence to lean on Washington again this week in this matchup, with Patrick Surtain likely shadowing Brian Thomas Jr. It won't be an easy matchup, though. Last year, Denver allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target and the eighth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers.

Drake London will be a tough player to depend upon with Cooper Rush under center. In Week 1, with Cooper Rush operating as Captain Checkdown, London had only a 13.6% target share, 29 receiving yards (1.21 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 21.4% first-read share. There's nothing good to see here. Nothing at all. Rush is a below-league average passer and it showed in Week 1. We'll see if he can bounce back in Week 2 against a Carolina secondary that was leaky in Week 1. Last week, Carolina allowed the sixth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in passer rating allowed.

Tee Higgins had a quiet week in Week 1 as the WR41 in fantasy. Higgins had a 17.1% target share, 59 receiving yards (1.90 YPRR), zero red zone targets, two deep targets, and an 18.5% first-read share (second on the team). I know Houston allowed the second-most fantasy points per target and the fourth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1, but I don't expect this to be a wonderful matchup for Higgins in Week 2. Last year, Houston allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Higgins has the talent and quarterback play to outkick a tough matchup, but don't expect a massive stat line.

Tetairoa McMillanÂ had a solid showing in Week 1 as the WR32 in fantasy. He was second on the team with a 21.1% target share while tying for the team lead in first-read share with 27.3%. McMillan finished with 75 receiving yards (1.92 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target. In Week 1, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (67.4%). Last year, in Weeks 13-19 against single high, McMillan had a 25% target per route run rate and 2.17 YPRR. In Week 1, against single high, McMillan had only a 13% target-per-route run rate and 0.65 YPRR. I'm not overreacting to his meh usage against this coverage last week. He should see plenty of volume this week to outkick what could be a tougher matchup if Atlanta's secondary can continue what they put on film in Week 1. Last week, Atlanta allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, it happened in Week 1. DJ Turner shadowed Emeka Egbuka. Turner followed Egbuka on 69% of his routes and limited him to 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Egbuka was the WR29 for the week, seeing a 21.4% target share with 63 receiving yards (2.17 YPRR), one deep target, and a team-leading 25% first-read share. Egbuka could have a wonderful game in Week 2 as the tip of the passing spear for Baker Mayfield, who should be on the warpath against his former team. In Week 1, the Browns allowed the eighth-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Jaylen Waddle had a horrible beginning to his Denver tenure in Week 1. He led the team with a 78.8% route share but saw only a 10.7% target share and 14.3% first-read share as he finished with one reception for two yards. Bo Nix played terribly in Week 1, and Davis Webb stumbled out of the blocks as a playcaller. I'm not laying this pitiful performance at the feet of Waddle. The entire Denver offense was on life support in Week 1. It won't get any easier in Week 2 for them, but I expect (or hope) that they will look at least serviceable this week. In Week 1, Jacksonville utilized two high with 56.7% of their defensive snaps. In 2024-2025, Waddle, against two high, had a 21% target-per-route run rate and 1.87 YPRR. If Nix can get him the ball, Waddle should have a bounce-back week, but I don't expect it to be a massive stat line. Last year, the Jags allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Luther Burden had a quiet week, considering his team put up 59 points in Week 1 as the WR37 in fantasy. Burden had a 17.2% target share, 63 receiving yards (2.42 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 27.8% first-read share (second on the team). Burden ran 53.8% of his routes from the slot. We'll see if his usage increases in Week 2, but the matchup is solid. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two-high, Burden led the team with a 25% target-per-route run rate while posting 1.88 yards per route run (second-best). Burden could be called upon more this week. Another staple of Flores' defense is the blitz. In Week 1, Flores dialed up blitz at an insane 73.9% clip. Last year, against the blitz, Burden was fourth on the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate, but he was only a part-time player. That could change in 2026. Burden won't have it easy, though. Last year, Minnesota allowed the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to opposing slot receivers.

Jameson Williams had a ROUGH Week 1 performance, and that's putting it kindly as the WR44 in fantasy scoring. Williams had a 23.1% target share and a fantastic 36% first-read share, but he had two drops and secured only one of his three contested targets. He also had one red zone target and two deep targets. The big takeaway is that his utilization was WONDERFUL, but Williams produced a wet-fart stat line with 45 scoreless receiving yards because of a bad game. This week he'll face a Bills' secondary that utilized two high at the eighth-highest rate in Week 1 (61.9%). Last year, against two high, Williams saw his TPRR fall from 22% (versus single high) to 16% while his yards per route run remained static against both coverage types at 2.15. The drop in usage in the offense is notable, but his strong efficiency against two-high is a positive indicator. One thing that will also be working against Williams in this matchup is possible shadow coverage from Christian Benford. Benford followed Nico Collins on 93.9% of his routes in Week 1, but he allowed Collins to secure six of his nine targets in his coverage for 66 yards and a score. This doesn't tell the entire story for Benford, though, as he also had a 75% blanketed rate against Collins, which is strong. Last year, Benford followed Ja'Marr Chase, Chris Olave, Tetairoa McMillan, Tyreek Hill, Drake London, D.K. Metcalf, Nico Collins, and AJ Brown on at least 60% of their routes. Only McMillan and London surpassed 60 receiving yards in his coverage, and only Olave and Hill scored touchdowns. I don't expect a massive game from Williams in Week 2.

In Week 1, Adams struggled mightily as a fantasy producer because his quarterback couldn't deliver catchable targets. He had a 66.7% catchable target rate which isn't horrible, but it's definitely not great. Adams had a 21.4% target share and 28.6% first-read share in Week 1, which he turned into three receptions and 26 receiving yards (1.30 YPRR). Adams didn't see a red zone or deep target in Week 1. I'm willing to roll Adams out there again depending upon my options in Week 2. He'll face a Giants' secondary that just held CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and company to the tenth-fewest fantasy points per target and the fourth-fewest yards per target on the perimeter.

Terry McLaurin had a horrible Week 1 against a stout Philly secondary. McLaurin finished with only two receptions and 14 receiving yards. He drew an 11.8% target share with 0.40 yards per route run, one red zone target, and a 17.4% first-read share. This is a wonderful bounceback spot for McLaurin in Week 2. Last week, Dallas utilized single high with 54.5% of their defensive snaps. Last year, against single high, McLaurin's target per route run rate rose from 20% (against two high) to 28% as he churned out a stellar 2.49 yards per route run. I'm not scared of this Dallas secondary after they allowed the 13th-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1 and ranked 19th in yards per target against the position.

HELLO HELLO HELLO JALEN COKER! Cokeheads unite! Week 1 was our day. It was wonderful to see Coker balling out as the WR1 overall in fantasy for Week 1. Among all wideouts in Week 1 with at least 20 routes, Coker was tenth in separation score and 15th in route win rate. Coker has the talent to succeed this season. That much is very true. Will he be Carolina's leading receiver all season? Eh, let's pump the brakes on that, but Week 1 was a standout performance. Coker led the team with a 23.7% target share while tying Tetairoa McMillan with a 27.3% first-read share. Coker also had three deep targets and one red zone target, which tied or exceeded McMillan's usage in Week 1. Coker finished with 138 receiving yards (3.94 YPRR) and two scores. In Week 1, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (67.4%). Last year, in Weeks 13-19 against single high, Coker had a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.81 YPRR. In Week 1, against single high, Coker had only a 30% target-per-route run rate and 5.10 YPRR. Those are amazing numbers no matter how you slice it. We'll see if Coker can keep the party bus rolling in Week 2, but Atlanta's secondary could bring him back down to earth some if their Week 1 showing was indicative of how we should view them for the rest of the season. Last week, Atlanta allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. After one week of NFL action. I'm not scared of Atlanta's secondary, though.

Stefon Diggs had a solid start to his Washington career as the WR17 in Week 1. Last week, Diggs had a 26.1% target share, 55 receiving yards (2.20 YPRR), one red zone target, a deep target, and a team-leading 26.1% first-read share. Diggs ran 60% of his routes from the slot. Diggs could follow up his productive Week 1 with another solid showing in Week 2 against a Dallas secondary that allowed the seventh-most fantasy points per target and the ninth-most yards per target to slot receivers in Week 1.

Well, the process was right with D.K. Metcalf for Week 1, but it didn't work out. Atlanta heavily utilized single high just like I knew they would (67.4%), and Metcalf saw a 24.4% target share and 39.1% first-read share, but he fell flat with only four receptions and 40 receiving yards (0.98 YPRR). We're going back to the well this week with Metcalf against a Pats defense that utilized single high with 55.6% of their defensive snaps in Week 1. Metcalf could see shadow coverage from Christian Gonzalez in Week 2. Gonzalez followed Jaxon Smith-Njigba on 65.4% of his routes in Week 1, but Smith-Njigba roasted him, securing six of his nine targets with 103 receiving yards and a score. Metcalf isn't the same tier of receiver as Smith-Njigba, so I don't see him having the same success in Week 2. Last year, Gonzalez followed Emeka Egbuka, Jerry Jeudy, Tee Higgins, and Darius Slayton on at least 60% of their routes, and only Egbuka surpassed 30 receiving yards in his coverage (only Slayton had a receiving touchdown). I expect Metcalf to get featured again this week, but I struggle to see him popping off with a massive week.

Chris Godwin disappointed me in Week 1 considering the matchup. Godwin had only a 14.3% target share, 40 receiving yards (1.33 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 20% first-read share. It was only one game, but it's possible Godwin is cooked at this point in his career. In Week 1, among 72 qualifying receivers, he ranked 69th in separation and 52nd in route win rate. That's horrible no matter how you slice it, but it's only one game. We'll see how Godwin does with some more games under his belt. Godwin has another nice matchup in Week 2, as Cleveland allowed the most fantasy points per target and yards per target to slot receivers in Week 1.

Rome Odunze entered last week's game at less than 100% and it showed in his production and playing time. He had a 48.6% snap rate and 55.3% route share. I hope both of those numbers climb this week, but we'll have to monitor his practice reports. Odunze finished with only a 10.3% target share, 52 receiving yards (2.48 YPRR), two deep targets, and a 5.6% first-read share. If Odunze is healthy enough, he could see a substantial workload against Brian Flores' two high coverage and blitz heavy nature. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two high, Odunze was second on the team with a 24% target per route run rate and he led the team with 1.89 yards per route run. In Week 1, Flores dialed up blitz at an insane 73.9% clip. Last season, against the blitz, Odunze led the team with a 27.8% target share, 30% target per route run rate, and a 32.1% first-read share. My fingers are crossed that Odunze has a big game in Week 2. Last year, Minnesota allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

We'll see if Ladd McConkey plays this week after sustaining a rib injury in Week 1. McConkey didn't practice on Wednesday or Thursday of this week because of that rib issue, but he managed a limited practice on Friday. McConkey has been listed as questionable this week. Last week, in the first three quarters of the game, McConkey was almost the entire Chargers passing attack. Johnston had only a 13.3% target share, eight receiving yards (0.62 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and an 8.3% first-read share. The Chargers offense as a whole sucked last week, so I hope that Mike McDaniel and company see that what they were doing in Week 1 wasn't working. We shall see. I never assume any rationality with coaching anymore. If Johnston does get more work this week, with McConkey active or not, he should have success. In Week 1, Las Vegas utilized single high with 62.2% of their defensive snaps. Last year, in the 11 healthy games Johnston played, against single high, he posted a 21% target per route run rate and 2.07 yards per route run. Last week, Las Vegas allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers, but I'm not fearful of this secondary after only one game.

Last week, Matthew Golden came out firing as the WR17 for the Week with a 26.2% target share, 95 receiving yards (2.38 YPRR), three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 30.3% first-read share. This week, he'll face a Jets' pass defense that utilized two high at the tenth-highest rate in Week 1 (59%). Last year, Golden was more utilized against two high, with his target-per-route run rate climbing from 14% (against single high) to 21% and his yards per route run increasing to 1.60 (1.34 vs. single high). He won't have an easy matchup, but it's one that he can possibly overcome. Last year, the Jets allowed the eighth-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Deebo Samuel was also only a part-time player in Week 1. Samuel finished as the WR13 for the week, but he had only a 44.4% route share. He made the most of it with a 20.6% target share (tied for the team lead), 48 receiving yards (3.0 YPRR), and a 20% first-read share (tied for second on the team). Samuel got in the end zone while leading the team with three red zone targets. He also got his customary rushing usage, adding a carry for 12 yards on the ground. I expect Samuel to have another strong game in Week 2 against a hapless Miami defense.

In Week 1, Michael Wilson was third on the team with an 18.9% target share as he finished with 56 receiving yards (1.56 YPRR), zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 25.9% first-read share (second on the team behind only Trey McBride). I don't want to plug Wilson into a fantasy lineup in Week 2 against this vaunted Seattle pass defense. In Week 1, Seattle allowed the 11th-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Courtland Sutton also had a quiet Week 1 to begin the season as Denver's offense struggled against the Chiefs. Sutton finished with a 14.3% target share, 11 receiving yards (0.48 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 14.3% first-read share. In Week 1, Jacksonville utilized two-high with 56.7% of their defensive snaps. This coverage type isn't great for Sutton's outlook in Week 2. Last year, against two-high, Sutton's target-per-route run rate dropped from 26% (against single high) to 18%, and his yards per route run dipped from 2.32 (against single high) to 1.41. If you can, sit Sutton this week. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, it was nice to see that Josh Downs was a full-time player in Week 1 as he had an 88.7% snap rate and 85.3% route share, but the offseason narrative about him playing on the perimeter didn't come to fruition as Downs ran 82.8% of his routes from the slot. Downs finished fourth on the team with a 12.9% target share while ranking third in first-read share with 21.1%. He had one deep target but zero red zone targets as he finished with 37 receiving yards (1.28 YPRR, 10.2 aDOT). Downs is a low-end flex play with a tough matchup this week. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 13th-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Jakobi Meyers had a quiet Week 1 as Jacksonville crushed the Browns. Meyers had only an 8.7% target share, 40 receiving yards (2.50 YPRR), one end zone target (one score), and a 5.6% first-read share. Meyers was the WR28 in fantasy for Week 1. Last year, in this matchup, Meyers had a 19.4% target share, 45 receiving yards (1.15 YPRR), two red zone targets, one deep target, and a 23.8% first-read share. Meyers got more work with Brian Thomas Jr. seeing Patrick Surtain all game. I expect that to be the case again in Week 2. I don't know how successful Meyers will be, though. Last year, Denver allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

As I predicted last week, Michael Pittman Jr. wasn't heavily involved as Pittsburgh dealt with a single high heavy matchup, and I think that'll be the case again in Week 2. Last week, Pittman Jr. had only a 7.3% target share, an 8.7% first-read share, and 58 receiving yards (1.61 YPRR). He didn't see any red zone or deep targets. Atlanta heavily utilized single-high just like I knew they would (67.4%). In Week 1, the Pats utilized single-high with 55.6% of their defensive snaps. Last year, in Weeks 1-10 against single-high, Pittman Jr. had only a 20% target-per-route-run rate and 1.45 yards per route run. In Week 1, against single-high, Pittman Jr. had only an 8% target-per-route-run rate. I don't see Pittman Jr. being a massive part of the Pittsburgh game plan this week. Sit Pittman Jr. He's also dealing with a foot issue now. Pittman practiced on a limited basis on Wednesday before missing practice on Thursday and Friday. He has been listed as questionable.

Marvin Harrison Jr. is a sit until further notice. He was the high aDOT cardio king for Arizona. I don't even have words at this point. This is an insane way to utilize his skill set in this offense, and it's not fantasy-friendly at all. Harrison Jr. had only an 8.1% target share (23.0 aDOT) and 7.4% first-read share. He was out-targeted in Week 1 by Trey McBride, Michael Wilson, Kendrick Bourne, and Jeremiyah Love. At this point, Arizona should just trade him.

Khalil Shakir is a deep league flex only for Week 2. He returned to his usual role in Week 1 that we have seen him garner throughout his career, running 57.1% of his routes from the slot. Shakir had a 65.6% route share, a 20.7% target share, 50 receiving yards (2.38 YPRR), and a 20% first-read share (tied for second on the team with Dalton Kincaid). Shakir didn't get a red zone, end zone, or deep target in Week 1, which isn't surprising. He's an empty-calorie PPR flex that you hope falls into the end zone, but in this high-scoring environment, that could happen in Week 2. In Week 1, Detroit allowed the seventh-most yards per target to slot receivers and ranked 15th in fantasy points per target.

Well, Romeo Doubs didn't exactly have the start to his Pats career that he or we fantasy managers wanted. Doubs laid a goose egg in Week 1 as he failed to secure any of his three targets. With AJ Brown on the shelf, the Pats and Drake Maye will have to lean on him more in Week 2. In Week 1, he had a 69% route share, a 9.1% target share, and a 14.8% first-read share. He saw one red zone target and a deep target. In Week 1, Pittsburgh deployed two high with 57.7% of their defensive snaps (12th-highest rate). Last season, with the Packers against two high, Doubs saw his target-per-route run rate climb from 21% (against single high) to 23% and his yards per route run stay stable at 1.86. Doubs could operate as the Pats' clear WR1 in Week 2. After facing Cooper Rush in Week 1, I don't think there's much to take away from the Steelers against perimeter wide receivers, but last season against them the Steelers allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity. Doubs is a volume-based flex play in Week 2.

Last week, Jordan Addison had a quiet game. Addison had only an 8.3% target share, zero receiving yards, one red zone target, and zero first-reads. In Week 1, Chicago utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (60.5%). Since 2024, against single high, Addison has had an 18% target-per-route run rate and 1.66 yards per route run. Those are passable numbers, but they aren't something to get overly excited about. Against the Chicago secondary, it might not matter in Week 2, though. In Week 1, Chicago allowed the third-most yards per target and the most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Addison is a risky but intriguing flex this week.

Last week, Jayden Reed remained a part-time player for the Packers. Reed had a 55.2% snap rate and 63% route share. He had only a 16.7% target share, 20 receiving yards (0.69 YPRR), a 21.2% first-read share, one red zone target, and zero deep targets. With his limited playing time and standing as the fourth option in the passing attack, he'll remain volatile week-to-week for fantasy purposes. This is a decent week to look at him as a flex option, though. Depending on what your options are at the flex. Last year, the Jets allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the 13th-most fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Unfortunately, with Cam Ward's disastrous Week 1 performance, Carnell Tate's day against the Jets was sunk. Tate led the team with an 18.8% target share and 31.6% first-read share. He was only able to turn that into four receptions and 38 receiving yards (1.15). Even if Tate has a wonderful Week 1, I wouldn't have a ton of interest in playing him against the Eagles this week, but this entire passing attack is tough to invest in until we see signs of life from Cam Ward. Philly was stellar at defending against perimeter wide receivers last year, and they continued that trend in Week 1. Philly allowed the fifth-fewest fantasy points per target and the sixth-fewest yards per target to outside receivers last week.

In Week 1, Devaughn Vele finished as the WR10 in fantasy as Tyler Shough passed early and often, trying to keep up with Detroit. Vele's nine targets look nice on paper until you realize that Shough chucked it 56 times and Vele had a 16.1% target share with 69 receiving yards (1.25 yards per route run). Vele was second on the team with a 22% first-read share with one red zone and one deep target. The inflated passing volume helped puff up Vele's box score, but his per-route numbers were just okay. Vele is a decent flex this week, but the matchup is tougher. In Week 1, Baltimore allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers while ranking 17th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Wan'Dale Robinson also had a sleepy Week 1, with Cam Ward struggling. Robinson tied for the team lead with an 18.8% target share and a 21.1% first-read share (second behind Carnell Tate). He was able to turn that volume into only five receptions and 38 receiving yards (1.15 YPRR). Robinson didn't see a red zone or deep target in Week 1. I don't want to plug Robinson into any lineup in Week 1 despite Cooper DeJean (75% catch rate and 140.6 passer rating allowed) struggling out of the gate last week. I expect Ward to be in a blender this week, and those struggles to continue to tank the receiving options in this passing attack.

In Week 1, KC Concepcion had an 18.2% target share and 28.6% first-read share, which were tied for the team lead with Denzel Boston. Concepcion had a deep target and finished with four receptions and 43 receiving yards (1.95 YPRR). Concepcion was the WR51 for the week. He could have a more productive Week 2, facing a secondary that allowed the 11th-most yards per target and fantasy points from receiving yards per game in Week 1.

In Week 1, Alec Pierce had a 58.5% snap rate and 64.7% route share, which is about where I figured he'd be coming off a lost training camp and preseason as he made his way back from injury and surgery in the offseason. Pierce tied for the team lead with a 19.4% target share (27% TPRR, led the team) and led the team with a 31.6% first-read share. He had a 17.1 aDOT, which I don't think will continue throughout the season if he's going to continue to operate as the team's WR1. Pierce finished with 61 receiving yards (2.77 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target as the WR34 for the week. Pierce should see his playing time increase slightly in Week 2 as the team continues to ramp him up. He could be a volume-based flex/WR3 for Week 2 with a tough matchup. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target and the second-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Brian Thomas Jr.Â is dealing with a shoulder injury. He practiced in a limited fashion all week and doesn't carry an injury designation into this game. He opened the week with a limited practice session on Wednesday. Last week, he had only a 50% route share, 13% target share, 40 receiving yards (3.33 YPRR), and a 16.7% first-read share. Even if he was fully healthy, I wouldn't want to play him this week. Last year, when Denver and Jacksonville tangled, Thomas Jr. was shadowed by Patrick Surtain, and I expect that to be the case again this week. Last year, Surtain followed Thomas Jr. on 78.8% of his routes, limiting him to one target, one reception, and nine receiving yards. Sit Thomas Jr. this week. He'll likely get blanketed again by Surtain this week.

Xavier Worthy didn't do much with his opportunities in Week 1, but it's notable that he led the team with a 22.2% target share and 30% first-read share (7.0 aDOT). Worthy was only able to finish with 18 receiving yards (0.67 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target. Worthy could be the team's WR1 if this usage holds this season, which would be a passing of the torch from Rashee Rice to him, but it's just a one-game sample, so I'm not getting ahead of myself. Worthy could offer some flex upside this week against a pass defense that was ripped apart in Week 1 by Lamar Jackson. In Week 1, Indy allowed the most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Caleb Douglas had a strong Week 1 as the WR22 in fantasy. He was second on the team with a 22.2% target share, producing 94 receiving yards, a STRONG 3.13 yards per route run, and seeing a team-leading 35.3% first-read share. He didn't have a red zone target, but he did see a deep target. I don't expect Douglas to produce as a WR2 weekly, but his usage could easily make him a WR3/flex moving forward until he has to fight with Chris Bell for the target throne weekly. The 49ers aren't a frightening matchup for perimeter wide receivers, ranking 16th in yards per target and receiving fantasy points per game allowed to the position after Week 1.

Ladd McConkey left Week1 with a rib injury. He didn't practice on Wednesday or Thursday of this week because of that rib issue, but he managed a limited practice on Friday. He has been listed as questionable this week. His status is up in the air. Even if he's active this week, he's a risk to plug into a fantasy lineup, as any big hit to those ribs could knock him out of the game. In Week 1, in the first three quarters of the game, McConkey had an 85% route share, a 46.7% target share, 82 receiving yards (4.82 YPRR), two red zone targets, a 41.7% first-read share, and zero deep targets. If McConkey is a full-time player in Week 2 with a similar usage pattern to Week 1, he should rip the Raiders apart. In Week 1, Las Vegas allowed the third-most yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Tre Tucker is the only Raiders wide receiver who had more than a 60% route share last week, so he's the only Raiders receiver making the Primer this week. Tucker had a 13.3% target share, 27 receiving yards (1.0 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 16.7% first-read share. I've never been a Tucker believer. He's better off left on your bench this week. Last week, the Bolts allowed the 13th-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Denzel Boston secured a long garbage-time touchdown in Week 1 to finish as the WR23 in fantasy. Boston had an 18.2% target share and 28.6% first-read share. Both of those marks tied for the team lead. Boston finished with 59 receiving yards (2.19 YPRR, 28.7 aDOT), one red zone target, and two deep targets. Boston could have another solid Week 2 facing a secondary that was 18th in yards per target and 19th in fantasy points per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1.

Well, Dontayvion Wicks made the most of his opportunities in Week 1 as DeVonta Smith's running mate. He was the WR21 in Week 1 while seeing a 16% target share (third on the team) with 73 receiving yards (2.70 YPRR), an end zone target (one score), and a 23.5% first-read share. Wicks also led the team with two deep targets (21.5 aDOT). If Hurts is looking to go deep again this week, Wicks could have another nice day. Last week, Tennessee allowed both of their deep targets to be secured while giving up 62 deep passing yards (tenth-most). In Week 1, Tennessee allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per target and the second-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Cordale Flott and Alontae Taylor weren't a formidable outside duo for Tennessee in Week 1, allowing a 118.8 passer rating and a 75% catch rate combined.

Malik Washington operated as Miami's WR2 in Week 1. He finished as the WR58 in fantasy, seeing a 29.6% target share and 23.5% first-read share. Washington led the team with three deep targets, but he didn't see a red zone look. Unfortunately, despite the volume, Washington's inefficiencies have followed him into 2026 with only 53 receiving yards and 1.47 yards per route run. Washington is a deep league flex only and more so for PPR formats where his raw volume can play up a tad more. Sit Washington unless you're truly desperate for points. The 49ers allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to receivers in Week 1.

Keenan Allen was a full-time player for the Colts in Week 1 with a 73.5% route share (67.9% snap rate). He was tied for the team lead with a 19.4% target share and was second on the team with a 26.3% first-read share. Allen finished with 32 receiving yards (1.28 YPRR), one red zone target, and zero deep targets as he ran 72% of his routes from the perimeter. Allen is a middling flex play this week with a tough matchup. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target and the second-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, Adonai Mitchel had a 12.5% target share, a 76.9% route share, 60 receiving yards (3.0 YPRR, 19.0 aDOT), one deep target, and a 12.5% first-read share. He faces a Green Bay secondary this week that utilized two high at the highest rate in the NFL in Week 1 (80%). Last year, against two high, Mitchell had a 22% target-per-route run rate, but he had only 1.48 yards per route run. There will be weeks to consider Mitchell as a flex option, but Week 2 isn't one of them.

Last week, Makai Lemon was Philly's starting slot receiver (64.3% slot). While he only played 66% of the snaps, he had an 84.8% route share, so he was on the field when Philly was looking to pass which honestly is good for Lemon, but not great for Philly. If defenses are looking for a tell for when Philly is looking to pass, Lemon could be an easy one to spot with this split if his overall playing time doesn't increase in Week 2. Lemon had only a 16% target share while seeing only manufactured targets around the line of scrimmage. Lemon had a -0.25 aDOT with three receptions, five receiving yards, and 50% of his targets coming on designed looks. In a low passing volume offense, Lemon isn't even flex worthy with this type of usage. I hope his role continues to evolve, but if this is how his usage remains all season he'll be tough to trust even in a flex spot. Sit Lemon in Week 2.

In Week 1, Kayshon Boutte had only a 64.3% route share, a 5.3% target share, and 21 receiving yards (0.78 YPRR) as he was the field stretcher (16.0 aDOT). This isn't the matchup to consider flexing Boutte, hoping that he converts a downfield target to fantasy goodness. Last year, Cincy allowed the fifth-lowest passer rating, the tenth-lowest passing success rate, and the tenth-lowest completion rate to deep passing.

Mack Hollins had his moments in Week 1 with a 70% snap share, 50% route share, a 24% target-per-route run rate, 51 receiving yards, 2.43 yards per route run, and a 19% first-read share.
