He had one red zone target and one deep target. Hollins could be called upon even more in Week 2. In Week 1, Pittsburgh deployed two high with 57.7% of their defensive snaps (12th-highest rate). Last year, against two high, Hollins saw his target-per-route run rate jump from 18% (against single high) to 22%, and his yards per route run climbed from 1.48 (against single high) to 1.94. Hollins could be the clear number two option in the Pats' passing attack this week. Despite a tough matchup, he has some sneaky flex appeal this week. After facing Cooper Rush in Week 1, I don't think there's much to take away from the Steelers against perimeter wide receivers, but last season against them, the Steelers allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity.

I was shocked in Week 1 to see Kendrick Bourne handing a 21.6% target share (second on the team) and 22.2% first-read share (third on the team). Bourne secured all eight of his targets, churning out 75 receiving yards (2.59 YPRR) while seeing a red zone target. He was the WR17 for the week. If Bourne keeps this type of usage up, he'll have some flex-worthy weeks this season, but I don't think Week 2 will be one of those weeks. Last week, Seattle allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target and the fourth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers.

Chris Bell isn't startable in fantasy yet. He's only a stash as Miami ramps up his playing time. In Week 1, he had a 51.4% route share, a 7.4% target share, and a 5.9% first-read share. Bell could eventually be the clear number one target for this passing attack as we move through the season, but we're not there yet. Bell is a weekly sit until we see his usage trend up more.

Kalif Raymond popped off with a surprising stat line in Week 1 as the WR15 in fantasy. He had only a 60% snap share and 57.9% route share, but he saw a 31% target share and 33.3% first-read share. Raymond finished with 84 receiving yards, 3.82 YPRR, one red zone target, and one deep target. I don't know if he will or can repeat this type of production, especially with a limited route share, but it's possible that he can. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two-high, Raymond had only a 14% target per route run rate and 1.28 yards per route run, but this was with Detroit. In 2024, with the Lions and Ben Johnson against two-high, Raymond had only a 12% target-per-route-run rate and 0.67 yards per route run. The analytics aren't in Raymond's favor to continue his hot start to the 2026 season. If you're in a deep league or desperate for a flex, I get it, but in most formats and leagues I'm not starting Raymond in Week 2. The matchup could be fruitful if you do decide to turn to Raymond, though. Last year, Minnesota allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

This could be the breakout season for Dalton Kincaid that we've been waiting for. In Week 1, he finished as the TE5 in weekly scoring, but it was more about his wonderful usage that has me tossing out this breakout idea. Kincaid had an 80.8% snap rate (WOW!), a 68.8% route share, a 20.7% target share, 130 receiving yards (5.91 YPRR), two deep targets, and a 20% first-read share. Yes, you read that correctly. Kincaid was a full-time player in the Bills' offense. I know this insane efficiency won't last the entire season, but we just saw Kincaid lead tight ends last season in every discernible per-route metric that I care about, so while I'm expecting per-route regression, he will still be elite in these categories. Kincaid faces a defense that allowed the second-most receiving fantasy points to tight ends in Week 1 while also giving up the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position. Kincaid could crush again this week.

Sam LaPorta finished with a solid but not amazing stat line for Week 1 as the TE15 in fantasy. He had a 17.9% target share (third on the team) and 16% first-read share (third on the team) while posting five receptions with 48 scoreless receiving yards (1.45 YPRR). He didn't see any deep targets, but he did walk away with two red zone targets. This week, he faces a Buffalo defense that continued a yearly tradition of being amazing against tight ends to open the 2026 season. In Week 1, Buffalo allowed the ninth-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. I expect this will be another tough matchup for LaPorta, so temper your expectations.

Dallas Goedert crushed Week 1 as the TE3 in fantasy. He tied for the team lead in target share (20%) and first-read share (23.5%) while producing 77 receiving yards (2.96 YPRR) and two touchdowns. Goedert had two red zone targets and a deep target. He should have another banner game in Week 2 against a pass defense that allowed the seventh-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Last week, Isaiah Likely was the TE1 in fantasy, amassing 27.8 PPR points. He played only 50% of the snaps, but he had a 69.7% route share with a 27.6% target share, 78 receiving yards (3.39 yards per route run), and a 31.8% first-read share. Likely two touchdowns and four red zone targets. If he keeps producing like this, he will have been this year's late-round tight end that everyone should have drafted (him or Dalton Kincaid). Likely has a tough on-paper matchup with the Rams this week. Last year, they allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends, but this year's defense fell on their face in Week 1. I'll take those last year numbers with a grain of salt at the moment. Even if this is a tough matchup, Likely is seeing top-shelf usage in this offense when he's on the field. Usage and volume could easily outkick a possibly bad matchup this week.

In Week 1, Travis Kelce finished as the TE16 in fantasy. He was second on the team with an 18.5% target share and 25% first-read share. He finished with 71 receiving yards (2.96 YPRR), zero red zone targets, and zero deep targets. Most of Kelce's production in Week 1 came on one long chunk gain. Kelce could return strong TE1 production in Week 2 against a pass defense that allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends last season.

In Week 1, Juwan Johnson was the TE7 in fantasy, finishing with a 10.7% target share, a 77.8% route share, three receptions, 54 receiving yards (1.10 YPRR), and a 14.6% first-read share (third on the team). Johnson saw one deep target and led the team with three red zone targets. Johnson will walk a tougher road in Week 2 to TE1 production against a pass defense that last year allowed the 11th-fewest yards per target and the third-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

In Week 1, Mark Andrews was the TE20 in fantasy as he had a 70% route share and 71.9% snap rate. Andrews had a 24% target share, 49 receiving yards (2.33 YPRR), a 26.3% first-read share, and one red zone target. He could flirt with TE1 value in Week 2 with that continued type of usage, but it won't be easy. Last year, New Orleans allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

George Kittle was eased into the 2026 season in Week 1. He had only a 47.2% route share and 46.9% snap share. Kittle was heavily involved when on the field with a 29% target-per-route run rate, a 14.7% target share, and a 20% first-read share. He finished with one red zone target, 12 receiving yards, and 0.71 yards per route run. Until Kittle is seeing a more substantial route share, he'll be a touchdown-or-bust fantasy option at the tight end position. He could return TE1 value in Week 2, but it's risky starting him with the limited playing time. Last year, Miami allowed the ninth-most yards per target and the tenth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

With more target competition around him this season, Harold Fannin Jr. took a step back in the target pecking order in Week 1. Fannin was fourth on the team with a 13.6% target share and 7.1% first-read share. He had only two receptions and 21 receiving yards (0.95 YPRR). Fannin also didn't get any high cholesterol usage, as he didn't have any red zone, end zone, or deep targets. Maybe he bounces back in Week 2, but all of this was a concern for me entering this season. This offense and the quarterback play aren't good enough to support more than one, maybe two, receiving options weekly for fantasy. If Fannin is on the outside looking in weekly on that inner circle, it could be a long season for him. Last year, the Bucs allowed the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends while ranking 15th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Michael Mayer will be the Raiders' starting tight end again this week. Last week, he was the TE19 in fantasy. Mayer had a 77.4% route share, a 23.3% target share, 32 receiving yards (1.33 YPRR), one red zone target, and only an 11.1% first-read share. That first-read share is low, especially considering the lack of receiving talent around Mayer on the Raiders roster. We'll see if he gets a bump in that department this week with a better matchup incoming. Last year, the Bolts allowed the 11th-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Mayer could flirt with TE1 production in Week 2.

Dalton Schultz had a predictable down week to open the season against the Bills as the TE19. Schultz was second on the team with a 21.1% target share and an 18.2% first-read share. Schultz turned that usage into four receptions and 35 receiving yards (1.13 YPRR). He didn't have any red zone, end zone, or deep targets in Week 1. Schultz could have a bounce-back performance in Week 2 against a defense that struggled last year to defend tight ends, giving up the third-most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position. With Nico Collins out, I wouldn't be shocked to see Schultz operate as Houston's de facto WR1 this week

Last week, Jake Ferguson had a quiet game with a 66.7% route share, a 73.1% snap rate, a 5.9% target share, six receiving yards (0.25 YPRR), one red zone target, and an 8% first-read share. Ferguson could be busy in Week 2 against a Washington secondary that allowed the most yards per target and the most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends last season. Last year, in his two games against Washington, Ferguson finished as the TE4 and TE23. The TE23 finish in Week 17 last year, he played only 30.4% of the snaps. I wouldn't be shocked to see Ferguson finish as a TE1 this week.

Kyle Pitts is a tough player to depend on in fantasy while Cooper Rush is making starts. In Week 1, he laid a goose egg, and his playing time was suspect. Pitts played only 63.2% of the snaps despite having a 76.9% route share. He had only a 4.5% target share and 7.1% first-read share. The matchup is nice for Pitts this week, but I don't know how anyone has any sense of confidence plugging him into a lineup. Last year, Carolina allowed the second-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

In Week 1, Hunter Henry had a 77.6% snap rate, a 52.4% route share, a 9.1% target share, 26 receiving yards (1.18 YPRR), and a 9.5% first-read share. None of this screams "steam this tight end in Week 2." If you're extremely desperate, though, the matchup is interesting, which gives Henry "break glass in case of emergency" type streamer appeal for Week 2. Last year, Pittsburgh allowed the fifth-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

In Week 1, Brenton Strange had a 13% target share, 23 receiving yards (1.64 YPRR), one red zone target (one score), and an 11.1% first-read share as he finished as the TE14 for the week. Last year, against this defense, Strange was the TE9 for the week. In that game, he had a 19.4% target share, 39 receiving yards, three red zone targets, a touchdown, and a 19% first-read share. I expect Trevor Lawrence to lean on Parker Washington and Strange again this week among his pass catchers. It won't be an easy road to walk for Strange, though. Last year, Denver allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends while ranking 19th in yards per target to the position as well.

T.J. Hockenson had a surprising Week 1 as the TE9 for the week. Hockenson had a 16.7% target share, 36 receiving yards (1.71 YPRR), one red zone target, a score, and a 20% first-read share. We'll see if that usage continues into Week 2. The matchup isn't great for Hockenson this week. Last year, Chicago allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target and the ninth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Last week, Pat Freiermuth was the clear starting tight end for Pittsburgh with a 70.3% snap rate and 72.1% route share. He finished with a 12.2% target share, five receptions, 46 receiving yards (1.48 YPRR), and an 8.7% first-read share. He had two red zone targets and a score as the TE6 for the week. That lowly first-read share scares me, though. I don't know if Freiermuth will see the same usage in Week 2 from a target share standpoint if he's often not the first read for Aaron Rodgers. The matchup is ok, but not amazing. Last year, New England was 17th in yards per target and 19th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends. Freiermuth is a low-end streaming option for Week 2.

Last week was one of those standout performances that we have come to expect during various points of the season from Mike Gesicki. He was the TE4 for the week as he led the team with a 20% target share, five receptions, 78 receiving yards (4.59 YPRR), a 41% target-per-route run rate, two red zone targets (one score), a deep target, and a 22.2% first-read share (led the team). The big issue is that Gesicki also had a 45.9% route share, so all of this production is extremely volatile and could have been heavily game plan specific for Week 1. Working in Gesicki's favor is that Dalton Kincaid ripped the Houston defense apart as the Texans allowed the highest yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity in Week 1 to tight ends. This is a continuation of giving up production to tight ends from 2025. Last year, in Weeks 12-18, Houston allowed the seventh-most receiving fantasy points per game and the 11th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. Gesicki is a viable tight end streaming option for Week 2.

Last week, Evan Engram had a 60.6% route share and 63.8% snap share. He saw a 14.3% target share and 21.4% first-read share as he finished with 43 receiving yards (2.15 YPRR) and a score. Engram had one red zone target and a deep target. He finished as the TE8 for the week. We'll see if he can keep the hot start up, but I have my doubts. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

In Week 1, Greg Dulcich finished with only two receptions and 18 receiving yards (0.82 yards per route run) despite logging a 74% snap rate and 59.5% route share. He didn't have a red zone target or a deep target. Dulcich had a disappointing 5.9% first-read share. I was high on him entering the season, as I expected him to be highly involved considering his 2025 per-route metrics and the lack of receiving talent on the Miami roster, but that's not how it worked out in Week 1. Dulcich is a sit until we see his role in this passing attack increase.

Terrance Ferguson remains only a dart-throw bench piece. In Week 1, he had only a 41.4% route share, 3.6% target share, and a 4.8% first-read share. This Rams tight end room could be a mess again in 2026. Only time will tell. Sit Ferguson until his playing time trends up.
Brock Bowers didn't practice on Wednesday or Thursday of this week. He managed a limited practice session on Friday and has been listed as doubtful. I expect Bowers to sit this week.

Maxx Crosby showed up in Week 1, tallying one solo, one assist, 1.5 sacks, and one tackle for loss. Crosby will look to add to his sack ledger against a Los Angeles Chargers team that appears to be having some growing pains adjusting to the new offense, and that may be without top receiver Ladd McConkey. Tap Maxx as a top-three play for the plus matchup against the division rival Chargers.

Devin Lloyd was excellent in Week 1 for Carolina, reeling off nine solos and four assists. Lloyd's nine solos led the league in Week 1 and serve to accentuate his upside now that he is no longer playing next to tackle vacuum Foyesade Oluokun. Treat the Panthers linebacker as an upside LB2 play for a tasty Week 2 matchup against the Atlanta Falcons.

Josh Hines-Allen went off in Week 1, racking up two solos, three assists, 1.5 sacks, one tackle for loss, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. JHA took full advantage of the tasty matchup in Week 1, but will have a tougher task in Week 2 against the Denver Broncos. Tap Hines-Allen as part of the LB1 conversation for the Sunday afternoon affair.

Dallas Turner showed up in Week 1, notching two solos, one sack, and one forced fumble. Turner played 84 percent of the snaps with Jonathan Greenard now longer in town and responded with a league-high 10 pressures in Week 1 (tied with Aidan Hutchinson). Turner already has an eight sack season on his resume and is entering his first season as a full-time starter. Tap Turner as a top-15 option going forward.

Greg Rousseau was unleashed in Week 1 and responded with four solos, two sacks, two tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, and one pass defended. Rousseau played a career high 80 percent of the snaps. The heavy usage is likely to continue under Jim Leonhard, as he wants his studs in Rousseau and Bradley Chubb to dominate the edge snaps. The Bills pass rusher should be rostered in all competitive leagues as a DL2 with DL1 talent and upside and should be treated as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Detroit Lions.

Leonard Williams impressed in Week 1, registering three solos, one assist, one sack, and one tackle for loss against the New England Patriots. Always one of the higher floor players with DT eligibility, Williams is also a strong DL3 play every week. When he has plus matchups like he has this week against Arizona, he becomes a DL2 option. Treat him accordingly for Week 2.

Travon Walker showed up in Week 2, racking up one solo, one assist, 1.5 sacks, and one assist. Walker was a massive disappointment in 2025, finishing with just 3.5 sacks, but is well on his way to his third double-digit sack campaign if he can ride this momentum to a bounce back season. Tap Walker as an upside DL3 play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Denver Broncos.

Oweh had himself a day in Week 1, making a statement with two solos, one assist, one sack, and two tackles for loss. Often lost in the edge rusher shuffle, Oweh has a 10 sack season on his resume (2024) and is fresh off a 7.5 sack campaign in 2025. Oweh has proven himself to be a DL2 play, but his rostership numbers suggest he is a DL5 type. Expect that to change somewhat during waivers, but there are other names managers may still prioritize over him. Tap him as a DL2 for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

David Bailey was excellent in Week 1, racking up four solos, one sack, and one tackle for loss in his NFL debut against the Tennessee Titans. Bailey paced the edge rushing room in snaps, sitting on the field for 70 percent of the team's defensive plays, a number that should rise as the coaching staff gets more comfortable with his mastery of the playbook. He was as good as advertised with the sack and six pressures, a number that tied him for the ninth most in the league heading into Monday Night Football. Tap Bailey as an upside DL3 option for a plus Week 3 matchup against the Green Bay Packers.

Ezeiruaku was excellent in Week 1, reeling off four solos, six assists, 0.5 sacks, one tackle for loss, and one forced fumble. Donovan is part of a deep Cowboys edge rusher rotation, but is a starter who led the team with 60.9 percent of the snaps. This is going to be a difficult rotation to have a share of, but Ezeiruaku is the best bet for consistent fantasy value due to his ability to set the edge and rush the passer. Tap Ezeiruaku as a DL3/4 piece where needed ahead of a plus Week 2 matchup against Washington.

Career season loading. Kwity Paye went off in Week 1, racking up three solos, three assists, two sacks, and two tackles for loss. Paye is splitting snaps with Malcolm Koonce opposite Maxx Crosby but will see his role expand if he continues to play well. Paye was signed to play closer to 80 percent of the snaps, but, of course, after the infamous Maxx Crosby to the Baltimore Ravens debacle, he played just 57 percent of the snaps in Week 1. Koonce played 52 percent of the snaps, while Crosby rarely left the field, playing 91 percent of the snaps. Tap Paye as an upside DL3 option, albeit with a bench floor for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Lukas Van Ness showed up in Week 1, registering four solos, one sack, and one tackle for loss. LVN is a starter while Micah Parsons is sidelined, and can strengthen his case to remain a starter if he can keep up the momentum he built in Week 1. He led the team with a 62.9 percent snap share against Minnesota. Treat Van Ness as deep league depth for now. Leave him on benches for Week 2 outside of ocean deep leagues.

Boye Mafe impressed in his Bengals debut, notching one solo, one assist, one tackle for loss, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. Mafe led the edge group with 64.9 percent of the snaps and should be locked into a starter's role for most, if not all, of the season. He does have Myles Murphy and Cashius Howell pushing him, but they will mostly split snaps with each other, with Cedric Hohnson also rotating in. Mafe is a DL3 with DL2 upside for as long as Shermar Stewart remains sidelined. Treat him as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Houston Texans.

Mason Graham was excellent in Week 1, stacking three solos, two assists, one sack, and two tackles for loss. Graham played 60 percent of the snaps in Week 1, pacing the interior defensive linemen group. Mason has significant upside and could quickly become part of the DL3/DT1 mix. For now, treat him as an upside DT2 but keep him on benches outside of DT leagues. Look elsewhere for Week 2.

Deone Walker impressed in Week 1, piling up three solos, three assists, one sack, and two tackles for loss. He played 64.6 percent of the snaps as the nose tackle against Houston and looks like he has taken another step. For now, he is strictly a DT league option (outside of 32 team leagues), but he has the tools and opportunity to become part of the DT2 conversation. Leave him on benches for Week 2.

Princely impressed in Week 1, starting in place of the injured Patrick Jones, racking up two solos, one assist, one sack, and one tackle for loss on 47 percent of the snaps. He is playing behind both Jaelan Phillips and Trevis Gipson, so the sack production will be sporadic and his weekly snap share will be inconsistent, but there is some ocean deep league upside here. For all of us who don't play in 32-team leagues, however, Unammielen should be avoided for Week 2, despite the tasty matchup against the Atlanta Falcons.

R Mason Thomas made an immediate impact for the Kansas City Chiefs, racking up one solo, one assist, one sack, and one tackle for loss on 53 percent of the snaps. The snap count puts him on the redraft radar as he only trailed Felix Anudike-Uzomah by one snap in his NFL debut. There is some reason for pause here as Ashton Gillotte was limited by injury, but there is no denying that R Mason and FAU are who the Chiefs would prefer to play more snaps. There is also the gamescript issue. The Chiefs were absolutely dominant, forcing the Chargers to throw early and often, which could have led to more snaps for the Chiefs' young pass rushers. With that said, the Chiefs are deploying looks where FAU kicks inside with Chris Jones and George Karlaftis, and Thomas man the outside; the package dubbed the NASCAR package should help Thomas push for the lead role on the edge opposite Furious George.

Jordyn Brooks was excellent in Week 1, racking up six solos and three assists. The consensus LB1 overall heading into the season, Brooks didn't disappoint in Week 1. The Dolphins linebacker should push for that title again this year and is a top-three play for this week's matchup against the San Francisco 49ers. Start him everywhere.

Jack Campbell did Jack Campbell things in Week 1, racking up a ho-hum five solos, two assists, and one tackle for loss. Campbell has set the bar so high that low-end LB1 production almost feels below expectations. The Lions linebacker is locked in as a weekly top-three option and is part of the top overall debate for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Buffalo Bills.

Carson Schwesinger showed up in Week 1, reeling off three solos, seven assists, and one tackle for loss. Carson is going to be part of the top-three debate all season, including this week against Tampa Bay. Needless to say, Schwesinger should be started everywhere.

Roquan Smith continued his IDP dominance in Week 1, reeling off five solos, six assists, one interception, and one pass defended. One of the most reliable names in IDP at any position, Roquan Smith is an easy top-five play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints. Start him everywhere.

Blake Cashman was cash in Week 1, tallying five solos, two assists, 0.5 sacks, and two tackles for loss. Cashman is a steady top-15 option for fantasy managers and is a weekly threat for LB1 production. Tap him as a top-12 play for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Chicago Bears.

Ernest Jones recording eight solos and five assists feels like another day at the office; that's how good Jones is and can be for his fantasy managers this season. Jones is part of the top-five discussion for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Arizona Cardinals. Start him everywhere.

Fred Warner impressed in Week 1, tallying five solos, six assists, one forced fumble, and one pass defended. Warner remains one of the elite options at the position and jumps into the top-three discussion for Week 2, thanks to a tasty matchup against the Miami Dolphins. Start Warner everywhere.

Zack Baun was excellent in Week 1, piling up seven solos, five assists, one tackle for loss, and two passes defended. Baun proved why he is still part of the LB1 conversation with his Week 1 production and will look to stay hot in Week 2 against the Tennessee Titans. Fire Baun up as a top-10 option for the plus matchup.

Foye wasn't his typical self in the tackle department in Week 1, registering just three solos and one assist, but added an interception and one pass defended to salvage his fantasy day. Oluokun is an LB1 option through and through, but, as tackle production like this week suggests, he is no longer the consensus number one IDP option he once was. Tap Foye as a LB1 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Denver Broncos.

Nate Landman impressed in Week 1, racking up five solos, three assists, and one pass defended. Landman is an easy LB1 option regardless of opponent and should be treated as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the New York Giants.

Edgerrin Cooper showed up in Week 1, racking up six solos, one assist, one sack, and two tackles for loss. Cooper will look to push to be part of the LB1 conversation but for now remains part of the weekly top-20 discourse. Cooper is a top-15 play for Week 2, however, thanks to a plus matchup against the New York Jets.

Giants linebacker Tremaine Edmunds was excellent for IDP managers in his New York debut, registering seven solos and one assist on Sunday Night Football. Edmunds had a strong start to begin his tenure as a New York Giant and can comfortably be viewed as a top-25 option who will be a top-20 play during the byes. There will be some inconsistency, but Edmunds will be one of the better options all year, including this week against the Los Angeles Rams.

Nakobe Dean was excellent in Week 1 for Las Vegas, reeling off five solos, one assist, one sack, two tackles for loss, and one forced fumble. Dean and Quay Walker instantly solve the Raiders' years-long issues at off-ball linebacker and should both be firmly a part of the LB2 conversation all season, with both possessing LB1 upside. Tap Dean as a top-25 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Sonny Styles had just three solos and one assist in Week 1, but added to it with one sack and two tackles for loss. Styles made an immediate impact for Washington's defense and should only get better from here on out. His weekly sack upside is going to keep him in the top-15 mix, and it shouldn't be long before his tackle production warrants his inclusion in the LB1 discussion. For now, tap Styles as an upside LB2 play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys.

Barrett Carter impressed in Week 1, reeling off five solos, three assists, 0.5 sacks, one tackle for loss, and one forced fumble. Carter was on replacement watch this offseason due to issues in coverage, but survived both the NFL Draft and free agency to resurrect his standing as an LB3 option. Carter has flashed LB2 upside and can get back in that mix if he can show some consistency. For now, tap him as a top-36 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Houston Texans.

Dolphins rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez was excellent in Week 1, tallying five solos and nine assists in his NFL debut. Rodriguez actually outsnapped Jordyn Brooks (though only by one snap) against Las Vegas, suggesting that he is more than locked in to an everydown role going forward. Rodriguez should already be rostered in all competitive leagues, but with this being Week 1, we are including names over our five percent cutoff to ensure no one misses out on roster changers like the ascending rookie in Miami. Treat him as a top-20 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against San Francisco.

Azeez is excellent in Week 1, notching five solos, three assists, and one tackle for loss. Al-Shaair should produce enough to be part of the top-25 conversation most weeks, but is more comfortably deployed as an LB3 option, at least for now. Treat him as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Payton Wilson started for the Steelers in Week 1 and responded with five solos, eight assists, and two tackles for loss. Wilson proved he could be a capable starter last season, and his near every snap role proves he will be a fantasy force this season. He is an immediate LB3 who will be an LB2 option during the byes. He has LB2 upside overall, so make the add in all competitive leagues. Wilson is not someone

Jihaad Campbell showed out in Week 1, tallying five solos, four assists, one sack, and one tackle for loss. Jihaad was a trendy breakout candidate this offseason and rewarded his fantasy managers immediately. The top-15 upside is real, but for now, continue to treat him as an LB2 with LB1 upside. Start him if you got him for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Tennessee Titans.

Divine Deablo impressed in Week 1, recording three solos, four assists, one tackle for loss, and one fumble recovery. Deablo is part of the LB3 mix during the byes, but outings like this remind us that he has deep league flex optionality even when no teams have the week off. Tap Deablo as a flex option for Week 2 against the Carolina Panthers.

Drake Thomas was excellent in Week 1, reeling off three solos, five assists, one sack, and one tackle for loss. Drake had 3.5 sacks last season and should surpass that number this season if he stays healthy. Thomas is an LB3 option who will double as a LB2 play during the byes. Drake is an LB2 waiting to happen; he just needs to show more consistency over a long stretch.  Tap him as part of the top-25 conversation for a plus Week 2 matchup against Arizona.

Demetrius Knight was excellent in Week 1, racking up five solos, two assists, one fumble recovery, and one touchdown. Knight will push to be part of the LB2 conversation this season, but should be viewed as more of an LB3 until the byes hit, even with his hot start. Tap Demetrius as an upside LB3 play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Houston Texans.

Bucs rookie Josiah Trotter made an impact in Week 1, racking up four solos, seven assists, one sack, two tackles for loss, one interception, one pass defended, and one touchdown. It was an electric debut for the son of Jeremiah Trotter, who immediately carved out a name all of his own for the Buccaneers. Trotter's excellent production highlights his immense upside, puts him in the LB2 conversation immediately, and solidifies him as an LB1 in dynasty.

TJ Watt was elite in Week 1, exploding for four solos, two sacks, three tackles for loss, one interception, one pass defended, and one touchdown.  Watt will look to prove that he is completely healthy and back to true form again this week in what projects as a plus matchup against the New England Patriots. Tap him as a top-five option in all formats.

Ventrell Miller was excellent in Week 1, piling up seven solos, three assists, one sack, two tackles for loss, and one forced fumble. It's a blistering start for Miller, who was expected to be part of the LB3/LB4 discussion for most of the season. However, his upside flashing production in Week 1 is going to solidify him as an LB3 and make him one of the hotter names off the wire at the position. Tap Ventrell as a top-36 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Denver Broncos.

Anthony Hill got the start with Cedric Gray still in concussion protocol and flashed with two solos, 14 assists, and two passes defended. 16 total tackles is highly impressive, even if 14 of them were assists. Hill is going back to the bench when Gray is healthy, but may have earned himself a larger part of Cody Barton's snaps with his performance. A wait-and-see approach is necessary here as Hill is only a Week 2 play if Gray is ruled out again.

Jack Gibbens impressed in Week 1, tallying five solos, two assists, and 0.5 sacks. Gibbens won the starting role over Cody Simon this offseason, and only poor performance is expected to be a threat to his job. Gibbens is nothing more than an LB3/LB4, but can become a serviceable, or even coveted, LB3 option during the byes. For now, treat him as an upside LB3 for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Seattle Seahawks.

Andrew Van Ginkel was excellent in Week 1, piling up two solos, one assist, 1.5 sacks, one tackle for loss, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. AVG continues to shine under Brian Flores and will be part of the top-25 conversation most weeks. For now, treat him as an upside DL3 play for Week 2's matchup against the Chicago Bears.

Dorian Williams showed up in Week 1, reeling off four solos, five assists, and one tackle for loss on 84 percent of the snaps. Dorian won the starting role over Kaleb Elams-Orr over the summer, and it appears that he will dominate the snaps alongside Terrel Bernard, at least for now. Williams is an upside LB3/4 option as long as he is starting. Utilize him in that fashion for what should be a busy Thursday night Week 2 matchup against the Detroit Lions.

Derrick Barnes dominated the snaps alongside Jack Campbell in Week 1 and responded with three solos, two assists, one sack, one tackle for loss, one interception, and two passes defended. Barnes played 86 percent of the snaps while Devin White played just 20 percent (Malcolm Rodriguez played 22 percent), and the pick on top of the tackle production is going to go a long way to keeping his role intact as White struggles in coverage. Barnes is a solid LB3/flex play that should be rostered in all competitive leagues.

Alex Highsmith started the season with a bang, notching two solos, one assist, two sacks, and two tackles for loss. Highsmith has been wreaking havoc opposite T.J. Watt for years, most notably during his 14.5 sack 2022 season. Highsmith should be rostered in all competitive leagues ahead of a plus Week 2 matchup against the New England Patriots.
Devin White is playing in a strict reserve role behind Derrick Barnes and should be dropped in shallower formats. Those in deeper leagues can hold if roster space allows. Look elsewhere for Week 2.

Signed as emergency depth following injury and suspension to their two standout rookies from 2025, old man Za'Darius racked up three solos, two sacks, and three tackles for loss in Week 1. He should have an expanded role going forward, as the 24 percent of the snaps he played in Week 1 would normally keep him out of the fantasy conversation in all but the deepest of leagues. Roster him as depth for now, with an eye on him becoming bye week filler worthy by Week 4.

Derwin James was excellent in Week 1, racking up seven solos, three assists, and one pass defended. Derwin remains a DB1 play for the 2026 season and will climb into the top-five discussion given the right matchup. He will have just that in Week 2 against the Las Vegas Raiders. Start Derwin everywhere.

Nick Cross was excellent in his Commanders debut, reeling off five solos, three assists, and two tackles for loss. Cross is in the weekly DB1 conversation but becomes a top-10 play when he has plus matchups, as he does this week against the Dallas Cowboys. Start Cross everywhere.

Quentin Lake went off in Week 1, exploding with seven solos, three assists, one interception, and three passes defended. Treat Quentin as a DB1 option for Week 2's plus matchup against the New York Giants. Needless to say, Lake should be started in every and all formats.

Jordan Battle was excellent in Week 1, tallying six solos and three assists. He played every snap, and with Dax Hill now playing on the outside, Battle is expected to dominate the safety snaps at the line of scrimmage for the safety group, raising his weekly floor. Tap Battle as a top-10 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Houston Texans,

Dillon Thieneman showed out in Week 1, flashing with eight solos, two assists, and one pass defended against the Carolina Panthers. Thieneman played every snap in Week 1 and will continue to get all the work he can handle for the Chicago Bears, even when Coby Bryant and Xavier Woods are healthy. He flashed his DB1 upside in Week 1, but should settle in as more of a DB3 who could push for the DB2 conversation during the byes. Treat him as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Minnesota Vikings.

Julian Love was excellent in Week 1, reeling off four solos, two assists, two tackles for loss, one interception, and one pass defended. Love is locked in the DB1 conversation, albeit on the lower end of the spectrum, when he has plus matchups, and is an excellent DB2 play all other weeks. Love is a DB2 option for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Arizona Cardinals. Start him where possible.

Caleb Downs showed up in his NFL debut, recording four solos, four assists, and one forced fumble. Downs spent 54 of his 61 snaps playing nickel (34 snaps) or deep (20 snaps), with just seven of his snaps coming in the box. Still, the box package is an encouraging development that could help raise his weekly floor. For now, keep him in the DB3 realm for Week 2, while monitoring his snap alignment.

Jaquan Brisker was excellent in Week 1, reeling off four solos, two assists, one interception, and one pass defended for the Steelers. Brisker played every snap alongside former All-Pro duo Jalen Ramsey. Jaquan is expected to have a heavy box role, as evidenced by the 57 percent of the time he lined up there in Week 1, putting him in the DB2 mix going forward. Treat him as such for a plus Week 2 matchup against the New England Patriots.

Kevin Winston showed up in Week 1, notching four solos and six assists. Winston is a DB2 option who is pushing to be part of the DB1 discussion. Count him as a top-20 play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles.

Amani Hooker impressed in Week 1, racking up six solos, four assists, and one tackle for loss. Hooker plays near the line of scrimmage while Kevin Byard patrols deep, so Hooker has weekly DB3 upside. Treat him as such for what should be a busy afternoon against the Philadelphia Eagles.

CJGJ played every snap in Week 1, responding with six solos and two assists for the Buffalo Bills. The mercurial safety has always been an IDP asset when he has been healthy and on an active NFL roster, and he looks poised to push his way back into the DB1 conversation. For now, tap him as a DB2 play for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Detroit Lions.

Evan Williams showed up in Week 1, tallying six solos and one assist. Williams has DB2 upside but will remain more of a DB3 play until he shows more consistency. Treat him as such for a tasty Week 2 matchup against the New York Jets.
Cam Bynum showed up in Week 1, racking up seven solos. Bynum is a solid DB3 with DB2 upside and should be counted as one for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs.

Jonas Sanker impressed in Week 1, reeling off seven solos, three assists, and one tackle for loss. Sanker played 66 percent of the snaps in Week 1, coming off the field when the Saints didn't need a nickel/slot back. Sanker's upside will be capped if he stays under the 70 percent snap share mark for the entire season, but playing the STAR role will provide him with some high levearage opportunities. Sanker is a solid depth piece who you can start during the byes, but you don't want to be starting him in Week 2, unless you play in a 20+ team league. Keep Sanker stashed but look elsewhere for Week 2.

Dax Hill impressed in Week 1, racking up seven solos. Hill has moved to outside corner full time, so he makes for an excellent CB1 candidate, but his weekly upside is likely capped. He will be one of the better tackling outside corners, so he should still have bye week value, but this will likely serve as a high watermark from solo tackle and possibly even total tackle perspective. Tap Hill as a CB1 but take another week before plugging him into lineups in DB leagues.

Marlon Humphrey was excellent in Week 1, reeling off three solos, one assist, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, and one pass defended. Humphrey has managed to stay in the DB2 conversation as a corner, and outings like this highlight why. Tap Humphrey as a DB3 option for Week 2 where needed.
Dane Belton is a DB3 play for Week 2 due to Minkah Fitzpatrick being sidelined with a groin injury. Plug him into lineups until the former All-Pro safety returns for the New York Jets.

Malaki Starks was excellent in Week 1, tallying two solos, five assists, one sack, and one tackle for loss. Starks played 25 percent of his snaps in the box, something that will help boost his fantasy value if the trend continues. Tap Starks as a top-25 option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints.

Andrew Wingard showed out in Week 1, tallying three solos, one assist, two tackles for loss, one forced fumble, one interception, and one pass defended. Wingard, having one of the standout IDP performances in Week 1, was on no one's bingo card, but that is not to say he hasn't shown flashes of his upside in previous seasons. For now, treat him as a DB3/4 or flex option for a plus Week 2 matchup against the Seattle Seahawks. Start Wingard where possible.

Justin Reid played every snap in Week 1 and responded with five solos, three assists, and one tackle for loss. His history suggests that he will settle in as a DB3/4, but he remains someone to monitor regardless of your roster needs. With that said, he does have a plus matchup on tap against the Baltimore Ravens, so feel free to fire him up as a DB3 option if you are cycling through waiver options post-draft.

Treydan Stukes was excellent in Week 1, piling up four solos, two assists, one interception, and one pass defended. Stukes played every snap for the Raiders, relegating Isaiah Pola-Mao strictly to special teams duties. He did his job and then some in his NFL debut and looks like a potential IDP star in the making. Tap Stukes as a DB3 with DB2 upside for a plus Week 2 matchup against a Los Angeles Chargers team that had its struggles last week.
Andre Cisco made an IDP impact in Week 1, tallying six solos. Cisco played 88 percent of the snaps alongside Dane Belton, who filled in for the injured Minkah Fitzpatrick.

Byron Murphy was excellent in Week 1, notching seven solos, one assist, and one pass defended. Murphy is one of the better tackling corners in the game and offers CB1 upside even as a number one corner. Leave him on benches where possible for Week 2, with an eye on starting him during the byes.

Zyon McCollum showed out in Week 1, racking up eight solos, one assist, one tackle for loss, and two passes defended against the Cincinnati Bengals. McCollum has flashed before, most notably recording nine solos against the New York Jets. Zyon's performance puts him in the CB league mix as a CB2 option, but he has not yet shown enough to trust as a DB3 outside of the byes. That being said, McCollum averaged as many fantasy points per game as Tyler Nubin and Grant Delpit last season, so the potential is definitely there. Keep Zyon stashed where possible but keep him glued to benches for Week 2, despite the tasty matchup against the Cleveland Browns.

Bryan Cook was excellent in Week 1, racking up four solos, two assists, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery. Cook makes for a solid DB3 option for Week 2, thanks to a plus matchup against the Houston Texans. Start him where needed.

Rookie safety Michael Taffee had himself a day in Week 1, racking up one solo, three assists, one interception, and one pass defended on 75 percent of the snaps. Taaffe surprised some by playing more snaps than supposed starter Dante Trader, who played just 47 percent of the snaps. Taaffe being locked into a starter's role puts him directly in the DB3 mix for the byes and the flex conversation otherwise. Start him as a DB4/flex option for what should be a busy afternoon at the office against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 2.

Calen Bullock impressed in Week 1, racking up five solos, one assist, and one pass defended. Bullock is viewed more as bye week depth at the current time, but that could change if he can keep up the solo production despite playing deep for the bulk of his snaps. For now, leave him on benches for Week 2 despite the plus matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rock Ya-Sin was excellent in Week 1, notching seven solos. Rock is a CB1 option for Week 2 and beyond, but is not someone to consider outside of the byes in 12 team leagues. Look elsewhere for Week 2.

James Pierre impressed in Week 1, registering four solos, one interception, and two passes defended. Pierre is a CB1 option who can fill in at DB during the byes. He is too boom-or-bust to trust over safeties most weeks, but has proven the ability to provide DB3 value in a pinch, especially in deeper leagues.

Quan Martin played just 38 percent of the snaps in Week 1, leaving him off the fantasy radar for the time being. Martin will be stuck behind Jeremy Reaves for the foreseeable future and is safe to drop outside of 32 team leagues.

Isaiah Pola-Mao looks like he is in a strict backup role for the Las Vegas Raiders. He lost the starting job to Treydan Stukes over the summer and played zero defensive snaps in Week 1. He is a drop in all formats, even dynasty leagues under 16 teams.
